    <title>I left New York and a six-figure job to move back to India. H-1B restrictions made it easier to walk away.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-31T00:14:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/left-new-york-moved-back-to-india-family-h1b-visa-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a88365f1d1a1d028ba11934?format=jpeg" height="1536" width="2048" alt="Disha Lamba is in an airport surrounded by luggage."><figcaption>Disha Lamba moved back to India in May 2026.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Disha Lamba</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Disha Lamba moved to the US to study in 2021, but she struggled with being far from her family.</li><li>She also didn't like some of the restrictions that would come with life on <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/h-1b-visa-big-tech-immigration-green-card-2025-8" data-autoaffiliated="false">an H-1B visa</a>.</li><li>In May 2026, Lamba left her job and moved back to India, a decision she sees as worth it.</li></ul><p><em>This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Disha Lamba, 28, who lives in Gurugram, India. The following has been edited for length and clarity.</em></p><p>I was born and raised <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/india-silicon-valley-bengaluru-under-pressure-2024-12">in India</a>. As an introvert, I liked being in my comfort zone, but my dad dreamed of sending me to the US for my master's.</p><p>His friends' children went to the UK and the US and achieved so much. He wanted the same for me. In 2021, at 23, I went to NYU for a master's in computer engineering. I'd only <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-to-nyc-at-22-lived-with-70-year-old-roommate-2026-8">seen New York</a> in movies, but I quickly fell in love with it.</p><p>I had a great life in the US, but decided to move back in May 2026, primarily to be closer to family. I also wasn't OK with the<strong> </strong>restrictions that come with <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/trump-h1b-visa-fee-100k-international-student-india-leaving-america-2025-10">the H-1B visa</a>.</p>
      <aside class="callout-box headline-regular ignore-typography">
        <p>This is part of our ongoing coverage of how the Trump administration's <strong>H-1B visa changes</strong> affect workers.</p><p>If you've been impacted and want to share your story, please fill out this <a target="_blank" rel=" nofollow" class="" href="https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdSZiitEC7pvevxnnssU37KZnaTt-kGq-4FhiHmXzWjNDfOAg/viewform?usp=dialog">short form</a> for the reporter.</p>
      </aside>
    <h2 id="bc6aa402-46f6-4593-a05e-db0bf7a41e3e" data-toc-id="bc6aa402-46f6-4593-a05e-db0bf7a41e3e">New York transformed me</h2><p>I owe a lot of my current personality to my five <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-to-new-york-city-biggest-surprises-challenges-2026-5">years in New York</a>. Managing things on my own in a new environment made me really ambitious. I became more confident and had a high sense of individuality. In India, I never thought about traveling to another part of the country, and I didn't realize I loved hiking before coming to the US.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8d9f6579f11f0a89f90555?format=jpeg" height="2411" width="2597" alt="Disha Lamba is standing in front of the NYC skyline."><figcaption>Lamba fell in love with New York after moving there.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Disha Lamba</p></figcaption></figure><p>America exposed me to opportunities. In India, while studying information technology at undergrad, I was interested in <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/phd-big-tech-job-meta-skills-2026-5">data science,</a> but lacked the confidence to pursue it. At NYU, I had good professors who spoon-fed me information about machine learning and data science, which really helped.</p><p>New York is a hub for conferences and meetups, and I attended many. At one event, I met a senior data scientist at CVS Health, who encouraged me to apply to his company. I landed a data scientist role there in 2024.</p><p><a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/job-market-reinvention-career-pivot-upskilling-2026-8">The job market</a> was rough around that time, and a few of my friends moved to other countries because they couldn't find jobs or secure visa sponsorship.</p><h2 id="3e953b45-de7a-4517-8099-59280188dce4" data-toc-id="3e953b45-de7a-4517-8099-59280188dce4">Living away from family was hard</h2><p>CVS sponsored my H-1B visa, and I was informed that I was selected in the lottery in March 2026. However, my plan had always been to eventually <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/move-back-to-india-get-work-us-visa-culture-shock-2026-3">return to India</a>, and by that point, I'd already decided.</p><p>I had a great life in the US — I was happy with my job and social life, and I had a six-figure salary, but I felt lonely.</p><p>When the clock hit 5 p.m., there wasn't anyone around to ask me how my day was. I had friends, but friends can't be your family. I kept having to organize my video calls with my mom — who's my best friend — around the time difference.</p><p>I <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-abroad-relationship-with-parents-changed-2026-3">missed my family</a> and realized I was much happier and content around them. I wanted to be there for big celebrations and support my parents during good and bad times. I feared being far away if something bad happened.</p><p>My second reason for wanting to move back was the visa restrictions. Once you're on an H-1B, you need a new visa stamp to travel and return to the US, and getting a stamping appointment in India can be a pain. Since the H-1B is generally granted in three-year increments, I felt there'd be a lot of ongoing visa management.</p><p>The H-1B can also<strong> </strong>make it harder to change employers, pursue additional income streams, or take a career break.</p><p>The <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/h1b-lottery-visa-working-amazon-building-life-home-family-america-2026-8">H-1B visa</a> has its pros, but I wasn't OK with the cons.</p><h2 id="407a760a-c513-4cdf-9e15-82d48d6612e9" data-toc-id="407a760a-c513-4cdf-9e15-82d48d6612e9">I'm exploring options in India</h2><p>I resigned from CVS and flew home to Gurugram, a satellite city southwest of New Delhi, to live with my parents and brother.<strong> </strong>I liked working in the healthcare industry, where I felt I could make an impact, and I liked my team and manager. I questioned my decision because I felt I was giving up a lot to move home.</p><p>In India, I can choose to build a startup, change employers, and do a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/category/side-hustles">side hustle </a>without worrying about visa restrictions. I decided to take a two-month career break when I returned to India, relying on savings. It's a luxury that comes from not being on an employment visa.</p><p>I haven't got a job offer in hand yet, but I think India offers similar career opportunities to the US. Big companies like EY, Mastercard, and American Express have offices near me.</p><h2 id="95ac41e3-9f12-489e-9935-4cd05dd51e00" data-toc-id="95ac41e3-9f12-489e-9935-4cd05dd51e00">I'm embracing the little things</h2><p>I miss certain things about the US. I used to love walking around after work and staring at the New York skyline, but where I am now, the sidewalks aren't as walkable, and the public parks aren't as clean.</p><p>But at home in India, we have house help, which means I don't have to cook or clean, so I have more time to pursue my passions. If you're earning well, you can live comfortably here.</p><p>I still get anxious about whether I made the right decision, but getting to hug my parents every morning reminds me it was worth it. Our family starts the day with a chat over a cup of green tea. The little things we take for granted are also the things that matter.</p><p><em>Business Insider confirmed she was employed by CVS. CVS declined to respond to a request for comment.</em></p><p><em>A State Department spokesperson told Business Insider, "Our embassies and consulates around the world, including in India, are prioritizing thoroughly vetting each visa case above all else."</em></p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/left-new-york-moved-back-to-india-family-h1b-visa-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-31T00:14:01Z</published>
    <summary type="text">Disha Lamba, who left her job at CVS Health in New York to move back to India, felt like she was giving up a lot when she left the US.</summary>

    <title>I outsourced 2 family dinners a week. Sometimes good parenting means doing less.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T17:18:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/meal-kits-whats-for-dinner-family-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8deecf3f7df8787cff3450?format=jpeg" height="4284" width="5712" alt="Woman cooking"><figcaption>The author signed up for a meal service twice a week.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of the author</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Deciding what to cook every night was one of the most exhausting parts of my week.</li><li>I started ordering meal kits for just two dinners a week.</li><li>Having fewer meals to plan has significantly reduced my mental load.</li></ul><p>There are a few questions in my household that irritate me more than "What's for dinner?"</p><p>I think it's the casual assumption that I have created a <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/new-year-meal-plan-dietitian-nutritionist-tips-longevity-protein-fiber-2025-12">meal plan</a> for the week, done all the food shopping and prep, and gotten dinner on the table at exactly the time everyone wants it, all while trying to accommodate my kids' likes and dislikes. Not to mention the cleanup after.</p><p>We are a <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/family-of-four-lives-in-one-bedroom-apartment-benefits-good-2026-4">family of four</a>, and just the idea of "What's for dinner?" can be exhausting. Every parent deals with this every night, but that doesn't make it any less of a pain in the butt, even when my husband helps out.</p><h2 id="ea2e660b-08f5-4de0-a7f5-d2aac03ba776" data-toc-id="ea2e660b-08f5-4de0-a7f5-d2aac03ba776">I tried a meal subscription plan</h2><p>This past spring, I was at peak meal-planning-overwhelm, when I remembered I'd gotten a card in the mail offering a discount if I signed up for a particular <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/guides/kitchen/best-meal-kit-delivery-service">meal delivery subscription</a> — one that we had used in the past right after my second kid was born — but hadn't tried in years. "Their food was pretty good," I mused to myself. The wheels started turning, and the next thing I knew, I had signed the family up for two meals a week.</p><p>The impact was immediate and incredible — for me, at least. Just having those two nights a week covered for dinner made such a huge difference in my <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/mom-invisible-labor-groceries-food-cooking-family-2026-5">mental load</a>.</p><h2 id="4e22947a-83a4-4b07-955a-6e394bdb52e2" data-toc-id="4e22947a-83a4-4b07-955a-6e394bdb52e2">Deciding what to eat is what bothered me the most</h2><p><a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-i-save-money-on-grocery-shopping-family-200-2025-7">Grocery shopping</a> was not my main inconvenience; it was <em>deciding</em> what to have for dinner each night, and then all the prep work. It felt like I was wasting so much mental energy on what we should have, did we have that too recently to have it again this week, does one child hate it so much that she won't eat it even though the other child loves it, and so on.</p><p>I could do more than two days a week, but then the service starts getting pricey for our budget.</p><p>Another thing I love is that meal delivery lets me try recipes I wouldn't usually make. If a recipe calls for spices or sauces I don't typically have in my kitchen, I find I'm less inclined to make it. But when every ingredient is sent to me in the exact amount needed, I'm all in.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8df97179f11f0a89f90a50?format=jpeg" height="4284" width="5712" alt="Food pan"><figcaption>The author is more willing to try new things because of her meal service.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of the author</p></figcaption></figure><p>I am not a gourmet chef. I do not toil over recipes of my own invention until I've perfected them. But I do know how to follow a recipe and cook the basics, and the meal delivery services I've tried make it even easier. Each recipe gives you step-by-step instructions and the exact amount of every ingredient. And if you can't stand cooking, some services offer pre-made meals that just need to be heated up.</p><p>These days, I am no longer irritated when someone asks, "What's for dinner?" I simply say, "Chicken burrito bowls," or "Pork stir fry with lettuce cups," and go on my merry way.</p><p>Do both kids love every meal every time? Absolutely not. But the subscription has lots of options every week, so I can easily find meals that work for everyone most of the time. Then I find it much less daunting to have a meal plan for the remaining nights of the week. And that to me is worth its weight in gold.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/meal-kits-whats-for-dinner-family-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-30T17:18:01Z</published>
    <summary type="text">I hated deciding what my family should eat every night. Meal delivery didn't eliminate cooking, but it removed the part that overwhelmed me most.</summary>

    <title>Meta goes on a PR blitz and updates privacy settings as venues restrict smart glasses</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T16:50:49Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/meta-smart-glasses-pr-problem-camera-privacy-led-light-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a91ed8279f11f0a89f92527?format=jpeg" height="2635" width="4220" alt="Meta glasses"><figcaption>Meta wants to change the public&#39;s perception of its smart glasses.<p class="copyright">picture alliance/dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Meta's smart glasses have a PR problem.</li><li>So the company is trying to calm consumer nerves with a new PR campaign and privacy settings.</li><li>Some event organizers and venues, meanwhile, are restricting Meta's glasses.</li></ul><p>The small camera installed in <a target="_blank" class="editor-rtfLink" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/mark-zuckerberg-meta-glasses-style-comfort-tech-wearable-fashion-2026-6">Meta's AI smart glasses</a> has become a problem for the company and the public.</p><p>Photos and <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/instagram-crackdown-meta-ai-glasses-pickup-rizz-videos-moderation-challenges-2026-8">videos captured by Meta glasses</a> have proliferated on social media, and not all of them are consensual. Clips of content creators harassing women and recording their reactions covertly have become a trend, raising concerns about privacy.</p><p>"Are you a secret code?" one male content creator asked a woman in an Instagram video. "Because I'm trying to crack you." Some social media users have dubbed Meta's product "pervert glasses."</p><p>It's all a bad look for Meta. So the company is making moves to get ahead of the negativity. It has recently publicized new privacy settings for its glasses and has launched a PR blitz to explain them.</p><p>Meta Chief Technology Officer Andrew Bosworth posted an Instagram video on Friday, for example, in which he explained how the smart glasses' hands-free camera works.</p><p>"We designed this camera to be noticed by the people around you, so in every pair of glasses we make, there's a capture LED on the front, and it lights up when someone's taking photos or videos for the gallery," Bosworth said.</p><p>Bosworth said the camera has no off switch. It stops working if people try to cover or deactivate it.</p><p>"We took this issue all the way across Meta, and we've been taking down content and even whole accounts connected to people misusing the glasses," Bosworth said.</p><p>Alex Himel, the vice president of wearables at Meta, also attempted to calm nerves on Friday in a Threads post. He said Meta's smart glasses will not allow users to record if the camera's LED light is blocked before or during recording.</p><p>"We're going to keep rolling out updates like this to make sure the capture LED can reliably alert bystanders when photos or videos are being captured for someone's gallery," Himel said.</p><p>While the company has suspended accounts that use the cameras to harass people, Business Insider's Katie Notopoulos reported last week that it hasn't been able to catch them all.</p><p>Meta has taken strides to make their smart glasses a must-have accessory. The company has partnered with megastars like <a target="_blank" class="editor-rtfLink" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/meta-glasses-facial-recognition-kylie-jenner-2026-7">Kylie Jenner</a> and Teyana Taylor, and it produced a star-studded Super Bowl LX ad to drum up hype.</p><p>As AI smart glasses become increasingly accessible, some event and venue organizers are taking a cautious approach with guests. <a target="_blank" class="editor-rtfLink" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/burning-man-meta-ray-ban-smart-glasses-recording-policy-guidelines-2026-8">Burning Man</a> told attendees at the 2026 festival, which starts Monday, that they can bring smart glasses, but must get consent before filming anyone. New York City nightclub Basement updated its no-photo-and-video policy to include smart eyewear.</p><p>"Anyone bringing smart glasses into the venue, whether wearing them or carrying them in a bag, will be asked to leave and may be permanently banned," the venue said in an Instagram post on Friday.</p><p>Organizers for the DEFCON Hacking Conference told attendees in July that smart glasses and similar items are prohibited.</p><p>In his Instagram video, Bosworth urged users to watch for the LED light that indicates the cameras are recording.</p><p>"Please remember," he added, "the light is there for everyone."</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/meta-smart-glasses-pr-problem-camera-privacy-led-light-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-30T16:50:49Z</published>
    <summary type="text">Meta is trying to calm the public's nerves around its smart glasses.</summary>

    <title>Google Maps has renamed Lake Ontario 'Lake America' for Americans</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T14:52:22Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/google-maps-lake-ontario-lake-america-trump-canada-trade-war-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a942f5145e6f385a516ab55?format=jpeg" height="2667" width="4000" alt="&quot;Making the Great Lakes Even Greater&quot; signage during an executive order signing in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026."><figcaption>Google Maps said it changed the name of Lake Ontario to &quot;Lake America&quot; after the US Geographic Names Information System, the federal government&#39;s official database of place names, did the same.<p class="copyright">Bloomberg/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Google Maps now shows "Lake America" to US users after Trump ordered the name change.</li><li>Canadian users will still see "Lake Ontario," while others will see both names.</li><li>MapQuest went viral for refusing to change the name, while Apple Maps still says "Lake Ontario."</li></ul><p>Google Maps has made the switch — for Americans, at least.</p><p>A search on the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/best-memes-trump-lake-ontario-rename-lake-america-name-change-2026-8">mapping app</a> on Sunday shows the name "Lake America" for the body of water adjoining northern New York and southern Ontario, known until very recently — and still to most — as Lake Ontario.</p><p>President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday that he said would "immediately" rename the body of water to "Lake America." Canadian officials have said they will not recognize the new name.</p><p>In a blog post, Google said it changed the lake's name after the US Geographic Names Information System, the federal government's official database of place names, did the same.</p><p>"Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the U.S., people using Maps in the U.S. will see 'Lake America,'" the company said.</p><p>Canadian users will still see "Lake Ontario," according to Google. Viewers in the rest of the world will see both names.</p><p>As of Sunday, Apple Maps still says "Lake Ontario." The company did not respond to a request for comment sent on Sunday.</p><p>Trump made the switch in retaliation after <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/smart-people-trump-canadian-trade-war-tariffs-reactions-2026-8">trade talks</a> between the longtime allies broke down last week. The Trump administration imposed an additional 50% tariffs on many Canadian goods on August 22. Canada then responded in kind. Trump is now threatening <a target="_self" rel="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/trump-canada-tariffs-americas-favorite-cars-toyota-chevy-honda-2026-8"><u>50% tariffs on auto</u></a> and steel imports from Canada.</p><p>Ontario Premier Doug Ford said in an interview with ABC News on Sunday that those tariffs would be "devastating on the US."</p><p>"A tariff on Canada is nothing more than a tax on the American people," he said.</p><p>Many Google Maps users wondered if the company would follow Trump's lead after the president announced the change. MapQuest, the original<strong> </strong>online mapping service that Google obliterated despite having a near 10-year head start, briefly returned to prominence last week by refusing to change the name of the Great Lake.</p><p>"We're not changing it," the company said in one post. In another, the company invited users to name the lake "whatever you want."</p><p>The stalwart "we're not changing it" post has more than 5 million views on X. None of the account's 24 posts in July got more than two likes.</p><p>Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister who bowed out of trade negotiations after he said the United States introduced "unfair" last-minute changes, wrote in a post on X that "naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario."</p><p>"The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari'io, which, appropriately, means 'the lake is beautiful, the lake is big'," Carney said.</p><p>Trump also renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America" shortly after returning to office, part of an effort to restore what he called names that honor "American greatness."</p><p>Google, owing to its <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/places-trump-renamed-gulf-of-mexico-lake-ontario-2026-8">policy of following GNIS designations</a>, also now refers to the body of water as the "Gulf of America" on Google Maps.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/google-maps-lake-ontario-lake-america-trump-canada-trade-war-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-30T14:47:19Z</published>

    <title>Sony accuses Anthropic of 'brazen campaign' to train Claude on its music — and wants up to $150,000 a song</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T14:12:42Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-claude-training-copyright-music-lyrics-sony-lawsuit-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a930e933f7df8787cff51f4?format=jpeg" height="3333" width="5000" alt="Claude by Anthropic"><figcaption>Sony Music and Warner Chappell filed a lawsuit against Anthropic on Friday.<p class="copyright">Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Claude seems to be a music fan.</li><li>Sony Music and Warner Chappell sued Anthropic on Friday.</li><li>The music companies said Anthropic trained its Claude AI models on stolen, copyrighted works.</li></ul><p>Sony Music and Warner Chappell want Anthropic to pay up.</p><p>The publishing companies filed a lawsuit against Anthropic in a Northern California district court on Friday. Anthropic cofounders <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/dario-amodei">Dario Amodei</a> and <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-meta-offer-ai-talent-war-poaching-startups-2025-7">Benjamin Mann</a> were also named in the filing.</p><p>"Defendants Anthropic and its founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann have conducted a brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale in order to develop, operate, and reap enormous profits from Anthropic's 'Claude' series of artificial intelligence ('AI') models," the companies said in the complaint.</p><p>Anthropic denied the accusations in a statement. "We disagree with the publishers' claims and we intend to defend ourselves robustly in court," the company said.</p><p>Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell Music said Anthropic collected "thousands upon thousands" of copyrighted songs, including 80s anthem "Eye of the Tiger," Marvin Gaye's "Ain't No Mountain High Enough," Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas is You," and Taylor Swift's "Paper Rings."</p><p>In the lawsuit, the publishing companies said Anthropic has <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-cut-pirated-millions-used-books-train-claude-copyright-2025-6">pirated their copyrighted works</a> through a range of methods, including two digital archives, Library Genesis and Pirate Library Mirror. In June 2025, a judge ruled that Anthropic downloaded over 7 million pirated books to train Claude.</p><p>"Among the many millions of books that Defendants torrented from these illegal pirate websites were books containing the lyrics and sheet music to hundreds or more of Music Publishers' copyrighted musical compositions, identified in Exhibit A. Those works include 'Livin' On a Prayer,' 'September,' 'Great Balls of Fire,' 'Ramblin' Man,' and 'Hallelujah,'" the lawsuit says.</p><p>As a result, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-ai-agents-risk-report-safety-mythos-claude-2026">Claude models</a> generate identical or near-identical copies of the copyrighted work in their responses to users, the companies alleged. In the lawsuit, the companies said training Claude on copyrighted content allows it to produce AI-generated lyrics that will ultimately compete with human-made songs.</p><p>Sony Music and Warner Chappell requested a jury trial. They're seeking statutory damages from Anthropic, including up to $150,000 for each composition it used to train Claude.</p><p>"Even the most revolutionary of technologies must develop within the bounds of the law, and Anthropic's Claude models are no different," the companies said in the complaint.</p><p>The AI industry has been targeted by a slew of copyright lawsuits since large language models like Claude and ChatGPT began to transform society.</p><p>Tech companies need troves of data to train their AI models, and go to great lengths to acquire it. Most recently, historians and archivists have accused AI companies of acquiring large numbers of antique books and feeding them into their LLMs, destroying them in the process.</p><p>Last September, Anthropic agreed to pay over <a target="_blank" class="editor-rtfLink" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-pay-1-5-billion-authors-books-copyright-settlement-2025-9">$1.5 billion to authors</a> to settle a class-action lawsuit related to pirated works. OpenAI, too, has faced <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-books-anthropic-training-human-authors-market-amazon-research-2026-8">several copyright lawsuits</a> in recent years, including one from The New York Times and another from Encyclopedia Britannica.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-claude-training-copyright-music-lyrics-sony-lawsuit-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-30T14:12:42Z</published>

    <title>I moved back into my childhood home in my 30s. I never planned to stay long, but now I'm finding it hard to leave.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T13:57:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-back-into-childhood-home-adult-30s-living-with-parents-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8f270c79f11f0a89f91194?format=jpeg" height="2934" width="3912" alt="Woman and her parents smiling in front of scenic mountain views"><figcaption>Moving back into my childhood home to live with my parents in my 30s isn&#39;t the setback I thought it would be.<p class="copyright">Meredith Schneider</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Four years ago, my cat and I <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-to-hometown-after-running-from-it-living-with-parents-2025-7" data-autoaffiliated="false">moved into my childhood home</a> with my parents out of necessity.</li><li>It's been nice to save money and bond more with my family during this stage of life.</li><li>This arrangement lasted longer than expected, and moving out feels like it's going to be tough.</li></ul><p>The day after Thanksgiving, I learned I'd have to move out of my beloved century-old, two-bedroom apartment in Kansas City.</p><p>My building had been taken over by a management company in another state. </p><p>Unfortunately, this wasn't the beginning of a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/what-its-like-living-canadian-town-movies-filmed-victoria-hallmark">Hallmark movie</a> in which the protagonist unites with her neighbors to successfully push back against a corporate takeover (all while finding love along the way).</p><p>Instead, I found myself panicking about my next move while grieving the comfortable life I'd been so proud to have built over the seven years I'd rented that space.</p><p>A few weeks later, my parents suggested that my cat and I move back into my <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-back-into-childhood-home-adult-40-with-family-good-2026-3">childhood home</a> in the suburbs nearby. As much as living with mom and dad in my 30s felt like it could be embarrassing or a huge step back, it felt like the best choice. So, I did.</p><p>I planned to stay for just a few months, but it's now been four years — and leaving feels more difficult than I ever anticipated.</p><h2 id="e6a05157-5cb5-49b2-8ead-852c15b1bf2a" data-toc-id="e6a05157-5cb5-49b2-8ead-852c15b1bf2a">Financially, this setup has been a blessing</h2><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8f25e979f11f0a89f91170?format=jpeg" height="1536" width="2048" alt="Woman and her parents smiling in front of New Years baner on fireplace"><figcaption>Living with my parents has been going pretty well.<p class="copyright">Meredith Schneider</p></figcaption></figure><p>My parents live in a home that they have been paying a mortgage on for nearly 30 years. It's much cheaper than anything on the rental market, and my financial contributions aren't even close to what I'd be paying if I lived elsewhere.</p><p>It's also been freeing not to chase roommates down for their share of the rent. I've cut back on my expenses even more by no longer paying for WiFi or electric bills, and doing laundry at home instead of a laundromat.</p><p>My parents have always purchased enough food for a full household, even when they were empty nesters. This means food is rarely in short supply, and my <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/strategies-tips-slash-monthly-grocery-food-bill-save-money-2025-7">grocery bill is less</a>, too.</p><p>Luckily, they also stock up on some great snacks and subscribe to a weekly May through October <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/reference/what-is-a-csa">Community Supported Agriculture</a> (CSA) box full of organic produce that I cannot get enough of.</p><p>To further contribute to the household, I like to offer support through physical labor and chores. Personally, I love to cook, bake, and run errands for the family. I also run errands for my grandmother, who lives close by, which helps me check in with her more regularly.</p><h2 id="963eedc4-67fa-4470-b463-082f0e761d58" data-toc-id="963eedc4-67fa-4470-b463-082f0e761d58">Our dynamic has shifted, and I'm enjoying getting to enjoy my parents in a new way</h2><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8f25e979f11f0a89f91171?format=jpeg" height="3024" width="4032" alt="Woman and her parents smiling in front of scenic mountain views"><figcaption>I&#39;ve experienced a lot of life now that I&#39;m in my 30s, which has helped my parents trust me to be independent.<p class="copyright">Meredith Schneider</p></figcaption></figure><p><a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/live-with-family-instead-of-longterm-partner-benefits-2026-4">Living with my parents</a> in my 30s is very different from when I was a kid or even a teenager.</p><p>I had been away for a number of years, living in other cities and on my own, and that independence has earned me more of my parents' trust.</p><p>They now realize I am too old for rules — for the most part. In time, they have backed down on strict curfews and specific chore guidelines. We've also been able to have important conversations around expectations.</p><p>I've made it clear that respecting this household and keeping my parents informed about my plans is still important to me, but that it might look different now that I'm older.</p><p>For example, when I first moved back, my dad was constantly checking in on me. It was difficult to deal with, especially because I'm a freelance creative with a varied social life and shifting schedule.</p><p>Still, I can understand a father worrying about their kid. A brief chat about my age and level of responsibility helped us find common ground and build trust around checking in as needed.</p><p>Sharing a space with my parents as an adult has also helped me see them as they are now, from a perspective that is so different and less selfish than the one I had in my adolescence.</p><p>I have gotten to work alongside them and admire the career people they are firsthand. I enjoy their respective skills and hobbies, and even the lively debates we stir up while watching a new TV show.</p><h2 id="af398dc5-0340-4809-8c21-fb92dfffbd3e" data-toc-id="af398dc5-0340-4809-8c21-fb92dfffbd3e">I didn't plan to stay long, but now I worry about how difficult leaving will be</h2><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8f25e945e6f385a51693e0?format=jpeg" height="3024" width="4032" alt="Two people sitting facing water in Hawaii"><figcaption>My parents have been pretty great roommates.<p class="copyright">Meredith Schneider</p></figcaption></figure><p>Moving back home wasn't such a step backward after all. I have been able to jump into the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/gen-z-gig-economy-mindset-corporate-america-2025-6">gig economy</a> full force, contribute regularly to the household, and spend time with family.</p><p>My "few months" at home with my parents has turned into four years.</p><p>Although I have plenty of savings that would allow me to move out and live comfortably, I've taken my time finding a stable living situation that makes sense for me.</p><p>However, leaving home and all its comforts will be a lot harder than I thought this time around.</p><p>Still, no matter where I end up, I'll continue to <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/lived-with-parents-whole-life-benefits-downsides-helped-our-relationship-2026-8">connect with my parents</a>, whether taking my mom to concerts or trying new burger spots with my dad. I will also still offer to pick up sticks from the river birches in their backyard that I made them promise not to get rid of.</p><p>Everyone's timeline is unique and circumstances are different. I feel lucky — not embarrassed — I've got family to fall back on. And my parents will (most likely) always be my favorite roommates.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-back-into-childhood-home-adult-30s-living-with-parents-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-30T13:57:01Z</published>
    <summary type="text">I moved back in with my parents into my childhood home in my 30s, four years ago. It's been going surprisingly well, and it's hard for me to leave.</summary>

    <title>My grandkids fight bedtime with their parents. They fall asleep in minutes for me, and I try not to be smug about it.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T11:58:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/grandmother-grandkids-bedtime-sleep-tips-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8f23bf3f7df8787cff3bcd?format=jpeg" height="1500" width="2000" alt="Grandmother rocking baby"><figcaption>The author has a knack for getting her grandbabies to fall asleep.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of the author</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>My adult kids often ask me to take over when their children won't sleep.</li><li>I follow the parents' routines while staying calm and adjusting to each child's needs.</li><li>Sometimes I walk out of the bedroom with a sleeping grandchild just minutes later.</li></ul><p>I must have <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/inherited-money-mistake-regret-2024-3">inherited my mother's</a> magic touch for putting kids to sleep. It drives my kids crazy. </p><p>While I was visiting my son and daughter-in-law recently, she confided that <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/family-evening-walk-bedtime-routine-calm-kids-2024-12">bedtime had become a nightmare</a>. I offered to give her a break by putting my grandson to bed. I was prepared for a struggle since we were at their house, and he knew his mom was in the next room. </p><p>We took him to his room after his bath to put on his PJs and <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/guides/parenting/best-sleep-sack">sleep sack</a>. It was already darkened and droning with white noise. After she left the room, I gave him a hug and kiss while softly telling him I loved him and that it was now time for dodo. I put him down, and that was that. He squirmed a bit, but I rubbed his back for a couple of minutes until he settled down. Then I sat on the bed opposite his crib and read on my phone until he fell asleep. No hassle, no crying, no standing up. </p><p>This is not the first occurrence. Frequently, my exasperated kids have relinquished naptime to me when visiting. It is understood by everyone that Grand-maman will put the <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-support-kids-back-to-school-mental-health-child-psychologist-psychiatrist-2023-8">children to sleep</a>. </p><p>I try not to react smugly to their parents' astonishment as I walk out of the sleeping child's room five minutes later.</p><h2 id="27a6652e-9486-4835-b40f-e673c7284956" data-toc-id="27a6652e-9486-4835-b40f-e673c7284956">Calm is contagious</h2><p><a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/rocking-like-a-baby-can-help-adults-sleep-2019-2">Rocking a baby</a> to sleep remains one of my favorite and calming things in the world. As a young mother, I would especially look forward to those breaks, justifying my taking all the time I needed to put my child to sleep and glean some much-needed serenity myself.</p><p>For babies, my strategies consist of following their parents' lead. I stay on top of their current routine and stick to their order of things. Bathtime, quiet time, <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/sleep-scientist-reveals-15-minute-daily-ritual-improve-your-sleep-2017-11">dark rooms</a>, a pacifier, a bottle, a soft blanket, or a special plushie are no-brainers. </p><p>After running through their usual preliminaries, I sit in the bedroom rocking chair, holding them just firmly enough to help them settle without restricting movement so much that it provokes a struggle. I create sensory rhythmic patterns with my breathing, humming, patting, or rubbing circles on their back. Usually, that works. If not, small adjustments like standing and swaying, or switching from rubbing to patting and vice versa, are often enough. Once I have found a successful method for one child, I stick to it the next time.</p><h2 id="74c772eb-d808-4bb6-8265-d116e62ef71d" data-toc-id="74c772eb-d808-4bb6-8265-d116e62ef71d">I am gentle but firm and use all of my tricks</h2><p>If they do start to fuss, it is important not to let it escalate to the point of prolonging the process. Sometimes, taking a break and trying again is necessary. I ask myself: Is he overtired? Not tired enough? When was his last sleep and for how long? Is he feeling well? Has there been an abnormal disruption that threw him off his routine? I let those answers guide my next steps. If the child is upset or unwell, I take him to another room to help him reset, dimming the lights and turning off anything noisy.</p><p>For older kids, negotiation is often necessary. I remind them why quiet time is important: we have more fun later when we're not grumpy. I offer to read a story or play a children's meditation or story from my phone. I lay beside them in a darkish, quiet room and intentionally take loud, deep rhythmic breaths to encourage them to mimic me. The younger ones usually fall asleep, but the older ones who have outgrown naps at least rest, which is always helpful.</p><h2 id="7597406b-c0b6-44ce-9286-1fc7e36e3a65" data-toc-id="7597406b-c0b6-44ce-9286-1fc7e36e3a65">Different strokes for different little folks</h2><p>It is important to remember that each child is different. Some like to be rocked, some like to be laid down with a back rub, and others like to stand and sway. I adapt to whatever works for them and stick to it. Consistency is key.</p><p>I usually wait until they are calmed down, then ease them into bedtime with whatever feels familiar and comforting. Sometimes that’s rocking and humming; sometimes it’s just staying close and reassuring them until they settle. If they resist, I keep it gentle and remind him that it’s bedtime and that Grandma loves them.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/grandmother-grandkids-bedtime-sleep-tips-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-30T11:58:01Z</published>

    <title>Russia is slowly grinding through the Donbas as Ukraine braces for a brutal fight over its last strongholds</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T11:39:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/russia-grinds-deeper-into-donbas-ukraine-braces-for-key-battles-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a9075773f7df8787cff45a6?format=jpeg" height="2029" width="2706" alt="Silhouetted person stands inside a damaged room looking out through a broken window toward a bright landscape."><figcaption>A Ukrainian soldier looks out of a window of an apartment destroyed by shelling in the direction of Kostiantynivka.<p class="copyright">Alex Nikitenko/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Russia is advancing slowly through the Donbas as Ukraine prepares to defend its last major strongholds.</li><li>Ukrainian commanders say the fight for Kramatorsk and Sloviansk could become brutal battles of attrition.</li><li>Analysts warn the outcome may hinge on Ukraine's ability to keep troops supplied under relentless drone and air attacks.</li></ul><p>There is a moment before the camera begins rolling when the young Ukrainian commander says, "History is repeating itself for us in the Donbas. Unfortunately." Then he falls silent.</p><p>A few minutes later, the man, known by the call sign "Fleshka," takes a seat on a weight bench in the garden of a house in an eastern Ukrainian village, just a 30-minute drive from the nearest Russian troops. Every morning, he benches 80 kilograms here before returning to the screens where he coordinates the destruction of Russian assault units through the live feeds from his drone operators.</p><p>"I hope it will be a long fight. This is our land, and we will fight for every meter of it," Fleshka says once the camera is rolling. A few meters away stands his comrade "Sascha," another unit commander with the 33rd Brigade. "It's going to be a brutal meat grinder," he predicts, describing a bloody war of attrition. "But I'm glad to be part of it."</p><p>Fleshka, 24, and Sascha, 26, belong to a new generation of young Ukrainian commanders helping lead the defense of the last Ukrainian-held bastions in the Donbas. Both have spent years fighting on the front lines. They were involved in the drawn-out <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/bakhmut-how-ukraine-lost-city-russia-won-hollow-victory-2023-12">Battle of Bakhmut in 2023</a> and later took part in <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-ukraine-audacious-military-offensive-kursk-russia-could-backfire-experts-2024-8">Ukraine's offensive in Russia's Kursk</a> region at the end of 2024. Today, each man is responsible for more than 80 soldiers serving in a combined drone-and-infantry unit.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a90674145e6f385a5169cb7?format=jpeg" height="1600" width="2560" alt="Masked person in camouflage pants gestures while seated beside an outdoor barbell bench in a wooded yard."><figcaption>&quot;Fleshka,&quot; a young Ukrainian commander, speaking with WELT in eastern Ukraine.<p class="copyright">Lysenko/WELT</p></figcaption></figure><p>The Donbas is comprised of the Luhansk and Donetsk regions. Russia has captured almost all of Luhansk, while Ukraine controls just under one-fifth of the Donetsk region, an area of roughly 5,000 square kilometers, about five times the size of Berlin.</p><p>The question is increasingly not whether Putin's army will seize the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in Donbas, but when.</p><p>According to information obtained by WELT from conversations with representatives of a leading European intelligence service, Russian forces could reach the outskirts of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk by early 2027. The two cities form the center of the last major Ukrainian defensive belt in the Donbas.</p><p>Intelligence officials predict that Russian troops could complete the conquest of most of the region by next year. The human cost of that campaign, however, would likely be staggering. Hundreds of thousands more Russian soldiers could be killed or seriously wounded in the process.</p><p>Since the start of the war in 2022, Russia's military has suffered around 1.4 million casualties, according to estimates by analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, including up to 450,000 dead and nearly one million wounded.</p><p>Military analyst Franz-Stefan Gady, author of <em>Attack: When War Comes to Us</em>, offers a somewhat more optimistic assessment for Ukraine. <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/russia-advance-ukraine-slowest-modern-war-100-years-analysis-csis-2026-1">Russia's advance</a>, he argues, is progressing at its slowest pace since winter. "At the current rate, Donetsk region would not be fully captured until the early 2030s," he says.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a9074fc3f7df8787cff45a2?format=jpeg" height="4284" width="5712" alt="Three uniformed personnel walk through overgrown debris beside a heavily damaged apartment building with broken windows."><figcaption>Ukrainian service members in the heavily contested city of Pokrovsk, an area of intense fighting in Donetsk.<p class="copyright">Alex Nikitenko/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><p>A slowdown, however, should not be mistaken for a stabilization of the front lines. In some sectors, Kyiv's military position is deteriorating. Russia enjoys local superiority in <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/russia-is-sending-swarms-of-cheap-drones-after-single-soldiers-2026-5">first-person-view drones</a> on certain stretches of the front, in some cases by a ratio of 10 to one. Meanwhile, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ukraine-built-glide-bomb-vyrivniuvach-cheaper-homemade-option-2026-5">3,000-kilogram guided glide bombs</a> continue to inflict heavy losses on Ukrainian forces in front-line areas.</p><p>Gady believes it's possible that Russian troops could reach Kramatorsk and Sloviansk as early as spring or summer 2027, but only under one condition. </p><p>"Russia needs mobilization if it wants to sustain or increase the current pace," he says. "Moscow is unlikely to do this before the elections, and if it does, Ukraine has no equivalent response available."</p><p>According to Gady, Russia's General Staff estimates that newly mobilized troops need around four months before they can have a meaningful impact at the front. A mobilization this autumn could therefore begin to shape events during the first half of 2027.</p><p>Col. Markus Reisner of the Austrian Armed Forces says Russia's summer offensive has so far fallen well short of Kremlin expectations. Nevertheless, Putin's troops continue to advance "slowly but steadily".</p><p>The decisive factor in the battle for the Donbas, he argues, will be Ukrainian logistics.</p><p>"The single most important capability influencing the fight for the Ukrainian defensive belt around Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is the ability to supply the defenders in those cities. If Russian forces succeed in disrupting those supply routes, Ukrainian defenders will be able to hold out only for a limited period."</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a90743979f11f0a89f91b0b?format=jpeg" height="4640" width="6960" alt="Camouflaged soldier walks along a rural roadside beside a burned-out vehicle under a cloudy sky."><figcaption>A Ukrainian service member in Druzhkivka, one of the three cities making up the fortress belt in Donetsk.<p class="copyright">Pierre Crom/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><p>Already, much of the resupply effort relies on heavy multicopter drones and <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ukraine-teaching-nato-troops-how-ground-robots-work-war-2026-8">uncrewed ground vehicles</a>. Russian forces are systematically targeting these systems while simultaneously attempting to prevent the reinforcement and rotation of Ukrainian troops.</p><p>Reisner's warning is stark: "If the Ukrainians fail to break this vicious cycle, the defensive belt will fall." Ukrainian brigade commanders also acknowledge that Russia ultimately possesses the resources required to conquer the Donbas.</p><p>"Of course, Russia has the potential," Vadym Krykun, commander of the Lubart Brigade, told WELT earlier this year. "It remains the second-largest army in the world. The question is how far Russia is willing to go, how much further it is prepared to mobilize its economy and its population."</p><p>Krykun has been fighting in Donbas for more than a decade. Russian troops first entered the region in 2014, and fighting has continued ever since.</p><p>As recently as last year, there were hopes that a settlement over eastern Ukraine might pave the way for a ceasefire or even peace. At the end of 2025, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed withdrawing Ukrainian troops from parts of the Donbas as part of a peace initiative, on the condition that Russia also withdraw and that the area be converted into an internationally monitored demilitarized zone, or "free economic zone." The Kremlin rejected the proposal, which was also supported by the United States.</p><p>The troops led by Fleshka and Sascha operate heavy "Vampire" and "Nemesis" <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ukraine-turns-heavy-bombers-into-supply-drones-for-dangerous-logistics-2026-6">bomber drones</a> in the Donbas that can strike targets up to 50 kilometers away. They are complemented by reconnaissance drones, drone-based mine-laying systems, and ground robots.</p><p>"Our primary focus right now is eliminating their drone operators," Sascha says. "We located the enemy, bombed the position, and mined the area around it. So I would advise them to leave their foxholes and get as far away as possible."</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a90678a45e6f385a5169ccb?format=jpeg" height="1600" width="2560" alt="Masked person sits on a stripped, burned-out car in a wooded roadside area with recording equipment nearby."><figcaption>&quot;Sascha,&quot; a young Ukrainian commander, is responsible for more than 80 soldiers in Donbas.<p class="copyright">Lysenko/WELT</p></figcaption></figure><p>His soldiers, he says, are doing everything they can to <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/inside-ukraines-war-robot-revolution-2026-7">keep Ukrainian infantry alive</a>. "The longer the infantry survives, the longer the cities hold."</p><p>Fleshka explains that the so-called "<a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ukraine-drone-kill-zone-is-getting-bigger-2026-6">death zone</a>," the area in which soldiers must expect drone attacks at any moment, has expanded dramatically in recent months.</p><p>The kill zone now stretches 20 kilometers deep in some places, and up to 50 kilometers in others.</p><p>"When they use <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ukraine-special-operators-doing-more-infiltration-as-kill-zone-grows-2026-7">small groups</a> and start moving, and we detect them, nobody wants to let them get away," Sascha says. "Our priority is to eliminate them. There are so many Russians that they simply do not care. I don't know, it's a complicated subject. We eliminate them without much difficulty, but there are just so many of them."</p><p>Sascha then describes the Russian tactic in greater detail.</p><p>"The enemy sends people forward one at a time. Ten groups essentially means ten individuals."</p><p>If one reaches the designated position, another ten groups are sent forward. Eventually, one gets through, then another, then another, until six soldiers have assembled and can continue advancing together.</p><p>"Well, let's put it this way: it's a good tactic. An interesting tactic. I haven't come across anything quite like it before," he says.</p><p>According to Gady, this method of gradual infiltration and attrition is central to Russia's approach. "Cities do not fall through breakthroughs or house-to-house combat. They fall through exhaustion."</p><p>Fleshka fears that Druzhkivka could be the next city to come under serious threat.</p><p>"They have shifted their focus toward Sloviansk. They are already fighting in Mykolaivka."</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a90738e3f7df8787cff4591?format=jpeg" height="3648" width="5472" alt="Camouflage-clad person with tactical gear sits at a desk with laptop and electronics in a dim room."><figcaption>A Ukrainian drone operator in Druzhkivka.<p class="copyright">Francisco Richart Barbeira/NurPhoto via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><p>Sascha also expects a fierce battle for Sloviansk. He insists that his men are ready. "It will be like Chasiv Yar. But how long did they assault Chasiv Yar? About a year, if I remember correctly."</p><p>He points to the terrain surrounding Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. "The landscape here works in our favor and against theirs. We hold the high ground and have cover. It will be a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/norway-lesson-training-ukraine-dont-get-stuck-kind-war-attrition-2026-8">brutal meat grinder</a>."</p><p>Experts doubt that a complete Russian conquest of the Donbas would necessarily persuade the Kremlin to enter serious ceasefire negotiations. "Putin will adjust his war aims depending on the condition of Ukraine's defenders," says Reisner.</p><p>Russia is presently targeting what he describes as one of Ukraine's Achilles heels: the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ukraine-western-missile-interceptor-supply-dropped-threefold-this-year-2026-8">critical shortage of air-defense ammunition</a>, particularly for Patriot systems.</p><p>"The first major attacks indicate that Putin plans to subject Ukraine to sustained <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/new-threats-air-defense-challenges-force-hard-choices-2026-3">large-scale strikes</a> this winter. He is following a strategy of exhaustion inspired by Svechin, the well-known Soviet military theorist."</p><p>Gady argues that, from Moscow's perspective, the Donbas may represent only an intermediate objective.</p><p>"The Donbas is an interim goal, not the final one. Russia's strategic objective remains bringing Ukraine back into its sphere of influence. According to Ukrainian intelligence, planning already exists for future operations toward Mykolaiv, Kherson, and Odesa, even if no timelines have been defined."</p><p>A genuine de-escalation, he adds, is politically difficult for Moscow.</p><p>"It would require scaling back Russia's war economy and explaining to the population why the war is being brought to an end."</p><p><em>This story, which first ran on WELT, comes courtesy of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which harnesses the resources of the company's newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces, and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from The Telegraph, POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms.</em></p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/russia-grinds-deeper-into-donbas-ukraine-braces-for-key-battles-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>I knew my job wasn't the right fit for me. It still took me a year to quit.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T11:21:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/quit-job-decision-financial-security-mental-health-effects-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a91baf345e6f385a516a58c?format=jpeg" height="1536" width="2048" alt="the author and her husband"><figcaption>The author knew she needed to quit her job, and her husband was supportive.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Kate Oczypok</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>My people-pleasing tendencies kept me in a job that wasn't the right fit for too long. </li><li>I prefer more structure and feedback than I was getting, and needed a change.</li><li>After quitting, family and friends have said I seem lighter and happier.</li></ul><p>As the oldest of five children, I've always seen things through. I've been the responsible one, the one who gets it done, and, most importantly, a self-imposed <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-to-stop-being-a-people-pleaser-2023-9">people-pleaser</a>. These are just a few of the reasons it was so hard to quit a job that I devoted a decade to.</p><p>As a <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/started-freelancing-penny-a-word-never-gave-up-2025-4">freelance writer</a>, it's sometimes hard to find work, let alone steady work. I knew I could count on this position, but I also knew my mental health was being affected by it. There was less structure than what I preferred, and it just wasn't a good fit for me or the way I prefer to work, which includes plenty of routine, organization, and feedback.</p><h2 id="a084f566-9f75-49f4-9f9a-25c4527dff09" data-toc-id="a084f566-9f75-49f4-9f9a-25c4527dff09">It took me some time to come to a decision</h2><p>I stuck it out for a while, constantly weighing whether to quit or stay. Staying meant a consistent income, continuing to contribute to my household, and having financial security (or as much as freelancing can give!). Quitting meant <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/money-saving-habits-feel-more-financially-secure-advice-sun-life-2025-5">no financial security</a>, and given my people-pleasing nature, I was terrified of leaving my other coworkers.</p><p>I was even more scared of what future employers would think about my decision. To quit or not to quit was a question I pondered for over a year. Since I was so indecisive and constantly worried about this choice, I knew my mental health was suffering. I was worried all the time, I had insomnia, gastrointestinal issues, and my often anxiety-induced epilepsy had reared its ugly head.</p><p>Finally, my husband and I talked, and he mentioned how he had been observing how upset I was. Earlier in the year, we had decided I'd stick it out until I found other work with similar pay. I had yet to find that other work, though, which made my decision even more nerve-racking. During our conversation, my husband talked about how he would support me if <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/quit-finance-job-moved-countries-swtiched-fields-africa-2026-8">I quit</a>, and we'd figure things out as we always did. He just wanted to see me happy and less stressed. That was very reassuring, but my perfectionism continued to rear its ugly head.</p><h2 id="cfddeae0-8f5d-406d-93d2-09d3b709c253" data-toc-id="cfddeae0-8f5d-406d-93d2-09d3b709c253">My husband said he'd supported my decision, and a therapy session solidified it</h2><p>During a late May therapy session, I was discussing this yet-to-be-determined decision. My therapist saw how exasperated I was and simply and bluntly asked: "What is keeping you there?" She also reminded me that <a target="_blank" href="http://businessinsider.com/investment-banking-professional-burned-out-pivoted-to-portfolio-career-cure-2026-8">people leave jobs</a> all the time for many reasons, and there was no reason to worry. It was a total lightbulb moment. I decided then and there that I was going to quit. The very next week, I left the organization.</p><p>It was a scary, yet oddly refreshing feeling. I felt free and excited for the next chapter. A tradition my husband has kept up for years is handwritten letters to me on my birthday and our anniversary. A lot of my July birthday letter talked about how he knew my decision wasn't easy, but he was proud that I did it. He said quitting was a brave thing to do, and he loved me even more for doing it.</p><h2 id="b4f4a918-0b5e-423e-9add-da9ba74fa005" data-toc-id="b4f4a918-0b5e-423e-9add-da9ba74fa005">After quitting, I've been happier and have had opportunities come my way</h2><p>Since I left the organization, I have had so many opportunities come my way. Naturally, most of my worries have dissipated, even though there is still some <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/big-purchases-financial-risks-economic-uncertainty-real-estate-careers-2025-6">financial uncertainty</a> as I finish out the year. Family and friends have said I sound lighter and happier. I've been writing regularly for a few publications, and now I have more time to pitch publications and search for jobs.</p><p>My decision was the best idea for me, as it helped with my mental health and made me more inspired and excited for what's to come than ever before. It also reiterated how my husband and I are a team, and sometimes when one of us is down, the other steps up, and vice versa. All in all, the phrase "you got this" was something I repeated multiple times throughout this process. Now, I'm looking forward to whatever comes next.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/quit-job-decision-financial-security-mental-health-effects-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-30T11:21:01Z</published>

    <title>I bought a fixer-upper for $347,000 and turned it into two Airbnbs. It went so well I turned the garage into two more.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T11:15:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/turned-first-home-and-garage-into-4-airbnb-units-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a9094e979f11f0a89f91c7e?format=jpeg" height="2025" width="1206" alt="Person stands smiling with arms out on a driveway in front of a beige two-door residential building."><figcaption>Vanessa Banh turned a garage on her property into two Airbnb units.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Vanessa Banh</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Vanessa Banh bought her first home but never planned on living in it.</li><li>Bahn turned the four-bedroom home into two Airbnb properties, then turned the garage into two more.</li><li>She said she'd rather make extra money than live in one of the units.</li></ul><p><em>This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with </em><a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@vanebanh"><em>Vanessa Banh</em></a><em>, 28, a former accountant turned entrepreneur who bought a four-bedroom house with a garage in Modesto, California, and turned it into four separate Airbnb properties. The following has been edited for length and clarity.</em></p><p>I feel like my generation is half and half on whether they <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/gen-z-how-i-bought-home-new-york-city-apartment-2025-9">want to own a home</a>.</p><p>Personally, I think it's really expensive now <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/baby-boomers-struggling-housing-costs-fixed-income-2025-8">compared to our parents' generation</a>. The cost of living and <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/wage-growth-below-inflation-affecting-american-consumer-sentiment-2026-8">our wages</a> compared to the cost of housing is just outrageous.</p><p>For me, I was always looking for different ways to get more money. I listened to a lot of real estate people and gurus, and thought owning a house was the way to go to build assets and real wealth long-term. So why not start now if I can?</p><p>I bought a house for $347,000 in 2022 as a fixer-upper and took my time.</p><p>It was actually a cash or hard-money loan-only sale. I had a friend who's a hard money lender, and he looked at the property, and he was like, "I can lend this for you." So we purchased it through him through hard money.</p><p>Then we were able to refinance it back out to a conventional loan within a month because it wasn't bad; it was just really old and needed some updating.</p><p>I knew later on I was going to turn it into a rental.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a9084d245e6f385a5169e53?format=jpeg" height="1000" width="2000" alt="Side-by-side view of a residential driveway and detached backyard building under a clear blue sky."><figcaption>A side-by-side image of the garage before and after renovation.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Vanessa Banh</p></figcaption></figure><p>If you want to buy a house through the conventional route, you have to live in it for at least a year before you turn it into a rental.</p><p>The renovations took a year and a half, so that met the criteria already.</p><p>We closed in May 2022, but we didn't really start working on the renovations until August. My dad and I handled the renovations, took our time, and finished in July 2023.</p><p>I was just thinking about a long-term rental, but during the renovation process, my dad had different subcontractors walk through and give us some ideas.</p><p>I was also listening to a lot of <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/real-estate-investing-buying-housing-market-advice-brrr-method-biggerpockets-2023-5">podcasts — "Biggerpockets"</a> and all that stuff — so I was like, "This could be an Airbnb."</p><p>Maybe six or eight months into the process, I thought, "Let's try to <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/quit-airbnb-delisted-home-hosting-bad-guests-2026-2">Airbnb this thing</a> and see how it goes."</p><h2 id="d4dfe947-f22e-42da-b126-d438b98aa02b" data-toc-id="d4dfe947-f22e-42da-b126-d438b98aa02b">My first two Airbnbs were successes, so I turned my garage into two more</h2><p><a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/renovatied-basement-into-in-law-suite-for-mom-photos-2026-8">Renovations cost</a> about $60,000. We had to replace the roof and add a whole new AC, so those were the biggest costs.</p><p>Everything else was just standard flooring, a new bathroom, new tile, and all that stuff.</p><p>When we were renovating the house, one of the subcontractors who my dad had brought up to help with one part of the rental said, "In this section of the house, you could literally make this its own little unit right here."</p><p>The layout was really perfect for it because there's already a door there, so all we had to do was just add a little stove and a little sink, and add a double lock on the door so it functioned as a separate unit.</p><p>So now there are two units in the house.</p><p>One of the units was rented out mostly for traveling professionals, which I didn't anticipate. Traveling nurses would come and stay for three months at a time — there was basically no vacancy. I didn't realize there was something called <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/real-estate-investing-strategy-midterm-rentals-cash-flow-property-portfolio-2026-5">mid-term rentals</a>. So I was like, "Wow, this is actually quite amazing."</p><p>I averaged about $3,500 to $4,500 in revenue. Cash flow was about $1,000 to $1,500 because my mortgage was about $2,000 and utilities and all that stuff was about $500.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a9093673f7df8787cff4711?format=jpeg" height="2128" width="1206" alt="Single-story house exterior undergoing renovation with open doorways, tools, debris, and a partially visible worker inside."><figcaption>The garage mid-renovation.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Vanessa Banh.</p></figcaption></figure><p>I had a garage on the property that was just collecting dust.</p><p>When I bought this house, I was already imagining how we could turn that <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/airbnb-two-car-garage-massachusetts-2025-6">garage into an ADU</a>. But it was more like, "How do I get enough money to build this out?"</p><p>I feel like the little unit in the back was working really well for me, and it seemed like there was a lot of demand for traveling nurses and traveling professionals.</p><p>My one-bedroom, one-bathroom unit was already going for $1,800, so I thought, if I can squeeze in two studios in the garage, I can get almost more than $1,800 times two.</p><p>It took me a few years of stacking cash. </p><p>After the renovation for the first two units was done, I started learning <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/canadian-quit-job-to-flip-houses-usa-regrets-2026-8">how to wholesale and flip homes</a>. I was learning and actively doing that, and then I got enough cash to finally be able to start the next renovation process.</p><p>Once my plans were all done and final, I got three bids from contractors and started the renovation in November 2025. I always hoped that I would finish the garage conversion by the end of 2026. We finished in January 2026 — my contractor moved really fast.</p><p>The contractor's bid was about $100,000. After it was completely done, I paid another $8,500 because of miscellaneous costs, the city fees, and the architect's design.</p><h2 id="9187caea-3f8a-43f6-95d5-26d651747eb1" data-toc-id="9187caea-3f8a-43f6-95d5-26d651747eb1">The construction debt will be paid off in a few years, but it felt like the right move</h2><p>I finished construction for the garage units in January, then I finished furnishing everything and getting it all ready for Airbnb by late February. In March, I started getting my first bookings.</p><p>For the first few months, I had a new-listing discount because if you have no reviews on Airbnb, it's harder for guests to book it. So to make it a little more competitive, I had a lower rate. I was bringing in about $1,600 to $1,800 per unit for the first few months.</p><p>But essentially, right now I'm getting about $2,000 each for the units, so I doubled the revenue I could make. </p><p>Of course, it also cost almost double for the construction because of the permits — I had to pay for two permits and all that <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/adu-living-backyard-pros-cons-2025-9">because it's two ADUs</a>.</p><p>I'm kind of paying myself off right now. I think it's going to take about two years to just pay that whole debt off, and then after that, it'll be fully cash-flowed.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a9093e345e6f385a5169efc?format=jpeg" height="2500" width="1875" alt="Modern studio room with a made bed, ceiling fan, kitchenette, wood-look flooring, and neutral decor."><figcaption>The interior of one of the garage Airbnbs.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Vanessa Banh.</p></figcaption></figure><p>I view real estate as a way to get ahead. I can absolutely live in one of my units, but if I can make money off of it — another $2,000 a month — I would rather do that right now. That's where my head's at right now.</p><p>I was like, "How do I optimize the current home that I have to make me more money?" Because I don't have a W-2, what can I do to help myself get into a better financial position?</p><p>I knew the first step was to own a home.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/turned-first-home-and-garage-into-4-airbnb-units-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-30T11:15:01Z</published>
