    <title>My sister and I were laid off around the same time. We started a small business together to survive unemployment.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T11:07:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/sisters-started-small-business-together-after-lay-off-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a90727a45e6f385a5169d6f?format=jpeg" height="721" width="961" alt="Amanda Leigh Lichtenstein and her sister in the parking lot of goodwill"><figcaption>The author and her sister run a small business, selling vintage items.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Amanda Leigh Lichtenstein</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>My sister and I were both laid off from our jobs around the same time as our parents died.</li><li>We decided to start a small business, selling vintage items, which is something our mom taught us.</li><li>The small business is helping us through unemployment and face the grief.</li></ul><p>When I walk into a suburban <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/frank-lloyd-wright-midcentury-house-designs-kits-lindal-ceder-homes-2024-5">mid-century house</a> with my sister, we're on the hunt for treasures that will make our customers happy — but we also like to marvel at the elaborate wallpaper in the bathroom.</p><p>We have time now to sift through the junk drawers and basement bookshelves. Within the last few years, we both were <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/laid-off-50-corporate-job-content-creation-2026-8">laid off</a> from our jobs as writers and editors. While we continue to fling our résumés into the ring, we keep ourselves busy at estate sales and thrift stores.</p><p>We come from a family of thrifters and estate-sale lovers; our mother was an avid collector with an eye for beautiful and valuable antiques. She taught her three daughters how to find treasures in the junk —what to look for, how to bargain, and which cleaning potions worked best to restore items to their former glory.</p><p>I've always enjoyed the thrill of the hunt, but I never imagined turning our shared love for vintage into a <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/rv-rental-company-retirement-plan-small-business-entrepreneurs-2026-8">small business</a>.</p><h2 id="58178240-776b-4c15-af32-8bf8749eca6e" data-toc-id="58178240-776b-4c15-af32-8bf8749eca6e">My sister and I were laid off</h2><p>I sensed a wave of layoffs coming in digital media before it happened. A strange mix of optimism and despair coursed through me as I tried to regroup. I quickly landed a new job, only to be let go from that role a year later.</p><p>Meanwhile, my younger sister had lost her job as part of mass layoffs at a major corporation. We were both reeling while grieving the loss of our mother and now also caring for our elderly father in our childhood home.</p><p>With the looming <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/sam-altman-openai-risks-ai-2026-8">threat of AI</a>, the job market looked bleak.</p><p>Layoffs disrupt and disorient. It's hard to know how to spend your time when there's suddenly so much of it. It's easy to sink into the couch and think your new job is just remembering to shower and watching every episode of "<a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/love-island-usa-couples-still-together">Love Island</a>."</p><p>Facing job loss — and the grief of losing both of our parents within six years — my younger sister and I first reviewed our mom's epic collection for items we could sell. We also started hitting estate sales, thrift shops, antique malls, and garage sales more frequently.</p><h2 id="5ec98561-f8b9-4470-bc6c-dd026d6e39a3" data-toc-id="5ec98561-f8b9-4470-bc6c-dd026d6e39a3">Starting a business together was the answer</h2><p>As we gathered more goods, I decided to make it official and established Travel Far Now Vintage, an <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/scaled-etsy-shop-48k-profit-in-four-months-using-data-2025-3">Etsy shop</a>, in 2023.</p><p>I handle most aspects of the business — packing, shipping, and accounting — and I rely on the keen curatorial eye of my younger sister, who can walk into any estate sale or thrift shop and score the most unusual vintage items hidden in the heaps.</p><p>Together, we found unexpected joy during some of the most challenging years of our lives.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a9072f73f7df8787cff458f?format=jpeg" height="1020" width="1366" alt="a table filled with vintage items"><figcaption>The sisters are always on the hunt for vintage items.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Amanda Leigh Lichtenstein</p></figcaption></figure><p>There's no shortage of tasks to fill the time — from sourcing to cleaning, listing to packing, shipping to accounting, posting, and connecting with new clients — the business keeps us energized against the lethargy of layoffs.</p><p>Consistency is key. While we continue to search for meaningful <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/job-market-reinvention-career-pivot-upskilling-2026-8">full-time roles</a>, running a vintage business keeps us alert, active, and curious about the objects we collect within an ever-changing marketplace.</p><p>Luckily, no two days are alike. There's always someone looking for that exact vintage object that connects them with the past.</p><h2 id="434336f1-be79-448e-9bf1-fe159dd549d0" data-toc-id="434336f1-be79-448e-9bf1-fe159dd549d0">The business has also helped us heal</h2><p>Running a vintage business is the ultimate crash course in grief, with lessons on letting go at every turn.</p><p>There's an alchemy to this work. By giving abandoned objects a second chance at life, I've developed a deeper appreciation for the fleeting nature of time.</p><p>I've come to think of myself as a "memory merchant," dealing in nostalgia through vintage objects and the stories they tell about our lives.</p><p>When a client reaches out to me about an analog Sunbeam timer for sale, it's not just about the timer, but about connecting with a core memory in their childhood kitchen. Hearing these stories helps me connect with my own memories and make peace with the past.</p><p>Our vintage shop is an ode to our mother — the ultimate thrifter and sifter — who taught us the ropes. When we're out shopping, we always hear our mom's voice in the aisles.</p><p>"Do you know what this is?" she asks with a twinkle in her eye. "Yes, Mom, we know," we answer, and continue scanning the shelves for more unique treasures.</p><p>Operating this small vintage business with my sister has strengthened our bond as we remember our mom together. The search alone is therapeutic, but it's also immensely healing to know we can breathe new life into old things.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/sisters-started-small-business-together-after-lay-off-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>I downsized from a house to a small apartment. I got rid of a lot, but kept one sentimental item.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T10:17:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-downsized-house-small-apartment-decluttering-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a90b2683f7df8787cff4807?format=jpeg" height="2365" width="3025" alt="the author holding a tupperware bowl"><figcaption>The author went back and forth about keeping a Tupperware bowl from his childhood while downsizing.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Jesse Gormley</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>I recently moved from a single-family home to a small apartment.</li><li>During the move, I had to sort through my possessions and decide what to keep and what to let go of.</li><li>I realized I didn't need most of my stuff, though I did keep a Tupperware bowl from my childhood.</li></ul><p>Recently, after a major change in my personal life, I relocated from a <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/median-usa-home-could-cost-1-million-by-2050-2026-6">single-family home</a> to a 660-square-foot apartment. Transitions are hardly ever easy. Among all the uncertainty that comes with moving from a large living space to a smaller one is figuring out what to do with all your stuff. It's a weird predicament to be in, standing inside what is soon to be your former house, surrounded by possessions and knowing that not all of them can come with you.</p><p>When I started packing things up, some decisions took all of two seconds. The television was coming with me. So were my clothes, kitchenware, and the handful of pieces of furniture that would actually fit in my <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/living-in-small-apartment-helped-spending-habits-money-saving-2026-8">new apartment</a>. Easy.</p><p>After that, though? That's when the real decisions get made.</p><h2 id="d3448fe5-af82-4299-bf0f-8cf233fe1080" data-toc-id="d3448fe5-af82-4299-bf0f-8cf233fe1080">I made three piles to help me decide what to take with me</h2><p>I found myself standing in the middle of the room holding things that had somehow survived every move I'd ever made. Empty iPhone boxes? Straight into the trash. Old moto jacket? That one stayed in my hands for a long bit while I tried to decide whether I still liked it or just liked the version of myself who used to wear it.</p><p>Before long, I'd created three piles: keep, donate, and one more — the one that kept growing, and growing, and growing. The pile of "indecidables."</p><p>As a kid, we had a very old-school, oversize yellow Tupperware bowl that served primarily as our popcorn bowl, but my mom used it at Christmastime to store her cookies. When I tell you this bowl is big, I mean you had to carry it with both hands, even as an adult. And I certainly didn't need it. I also didn't have a place to store it. It was in and out of the <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moving-smaller-house-decluttering-tips-2024-7">toss pile</a> more times than I care to mention.</p><h2 id="45dd80ef-2b35-45bd-93db-444f3c1a54b8" data-toc-id="45dd80ef-2b35-45bd-93db-444f3c1a54b8">Decluttering during the move changed my relationship with possessions</h2><p>Downsizing is low-key grief. You don't realize the invisible burden your possessions have been until it's time to part ways with them. Every box you tape shut is a decision. Every trash bag, a choice.</p><p>As I began settling into my new place, I figured I'd miss the stuff I couldn't keep. What really surprised me, though, was how quickly it all kind of faded from my consciousness. It made me wonder whether I'd been hanging onto all of it for all those years because I needed it, or because I hadn't bothered to stop to ask if I still did.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a90b29f3f7df8787cff4809?format=jpeg" height="4284" width="5712" alt="a tupperware bowl sticking out of a cabinet."><figcaption>The author realized the Tupperware bowl he&#39;d kept didn&#39;t fit neatly into his cupboards.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Jesse Gormley</p></figcaption></figure><p>A few weeks after moving in, I needed my drill to put something together. After searching high and low for the thing, I came to the horrifying realization that somewhere along the way, <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/family-of-five-lives-one-bedroom-apartment-downsized-big-house-2026-8">during my downsizing</a>, the drill had either been tossed or donated. I was pretty annoyed with myself at first, wondering what other important things hadn't made it to the new place.</p><p>The weird thing is, other than the drill, I couldn't recall a single other item that I actually missed. I guess I'd thought of all my stuff as just that: one big collective item. When I tried to break that image down into individual possessions, I began to realize that maybe none of it was nearly as important as I'd always thought.</p><p>Still, though, I did end up grabbing that oversize Tupperware bowl as I was leaving. The thing is, I can't really point to a single defining memory associated with it. It wasn't the bowl from my birthday party or the one my mom always mixed cookie dough in, or anything like that. It was simply...there. Filled with popcorn during <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/why-ditching-streaming-for-dvds-made-family-movie-night-peaceful-2025-12">movie nights</a>. Filled with Christmas cookies every December. It had been part of the background of my life for so long that leaving it behind felt stranger than finding a place for it in my new apartment.</p><p>However, I still don't know where to keep it. It doesn't fit comfortably in any cabinet, so it wanders from shelf to countertop to pantry. But every time I see it, I'm reminded that not every possession earns its place because it's useful. Some earn it simply because they've quietly been with us for the whole time.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-downsized-house-small-apartment-decluttering-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>I manage 10+ agents at Cisco. It doesn't mean longer hours, but the work can feel more intense.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T09:55:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/cisco-director-engineering-ai-agents-faster-work-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a91be8f45e6f385a516a5a8?format=jpeg" height="3891" width="5837" alt="Digital screen"><figcaption>Sergio Freitas said he manages 10 to 20 agents daily, which manage their own agents.<p class="copyright">Khanchit Khirisutchalual/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Sergio Freitas is a senior director of engineering at Cisco and oversees 10 to 20 agents daily.</li><li>Now that agents are writing more code, it requires more review, Freitas said.</li><li>While he's not putting in more hours, he said the work is faster-paced and can feel more intense.</li></ul><p><em>This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Sergio Freitas, senior director of engineering at Cisco, based in Lisbon, Portugal. His identity and employment have been verified by Business Insider. This story has been edited for length and clarity.</em></p><p>I started as a software engineer, became a manager, and currently work as a director of engineering at Cisco, with four teams based in Portugal.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a907f7879f11f0a89f91ba5?format=jpeg" height="4000" width="5333" alt="Sergio Freitas headshot"><figcaption>Sergio Freitas said that AI agents have changed the pace of work.<p class="copyright">Sergio Freitas</p></figcaption></figure><p>Software engineering has always gone through changes. There are always new technologies you have to learn, like programming languages or frameworks. Now, it's the way engineers work that's changing rapidly, and in the last year, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-coding-agents-tools-software-engineering-jobs-future-2025-6">it's changed significantly</a>. People have to adapt to that, and that can cause stress.</p><p>The biggest change came after frontier models launched at the end of last year, like <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-claude-opus-4-5-beats-every-human-engineering-test-2025-11">Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.5</a>. That's when AI really started to be embedded in our workflows, and we began delegating and working with agents to do software engineering. We were using AI before, but more for autocomplete and prompting.</p><h2 id="df36f426-62cc-4581-af8e-e886c8ed847e" data-toc-id="df36f426-62cc-4581-af8e-e886c8ed847e">Agentic AI has changed our work</h2><p>Our work as <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/great-coding-reset-ai-software-engineering-2026-7">software engineers has changed</a> from crafting the code to be focused on architecture, design, managing workflows and agentic orchestration. Engineers are shifting from manual work to becoming system architects and workflow orchestrators, allowing them to solve larger, more complex architectural problems.</p><p>The agents are like teammates and I manage 10 to 20 agents daily, which manage other agents. The number of agents they manage depends on the complexity of the task. The main orchestrator agent can spawn sub-agents to complete specific tasks.</p><p>They're always running and they're aware of collaboration platform notifications, GitHub pull requests, and other integrations when given explicit permission. For example, based on the description of a ticket in Jira, which is our project management and issue-tracking tool, an agent creates the code, and then that has to be reviewed by the person who owns the agent. It then goes through a review process, where at least two engineers have to review the code.</p><p>About four months ago, we moved into <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/what-are-loops-ai-engineering-tips-2026-6">loop engineering</a>, where, instead of the agent asking questions, it loops, or keeps working until it gets the final response.</p><p>Sometimes, depending on what needs to be done, the agent can ask for authorization to connect to certain systems or perform certain operations. More and more, it's autonomous, but strict guardrails remain.</p><h2 id="503a9d2b-5d3e-45c5-81e3-21a7fdff651e" data-toc-id="503a9d2b-5d3e-45c5-81e3-21a7fdff651e">I'm reviewing more work</h2><p id="503a9d2b-5d3e-45c5-81e3-21a7fdff651e">There's a lot of value in having AI work with engineers, but they need to be conscious about reviewing the code. Everything that gets delivered to production is the human's responsibility, not the agent's.</p><p>I'm not working more hours, but there is an aspect of AI that brings, in many occasions, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/companies-waiting-ai-productivity-boom-2026-6">more work to the table</a> because it can do more.</p><p>Cisco focuses a lot on security. So there are a lot of security scans you need to run, and conversations with the legal team that need to happen.</p><h2 id="81465112-5ef5-4853-bcda-613cbf989989" data-toc-id="81465112-5ef5-4853-bcda-613cbf989989">It's a faster-paced job</h2><p id="07d5604c-15ef-489c-abda-4c76cd70c7da">As engineers adapt to this new way of working, some initial fatigue comes from the ability to do more. You have to shift your attention a lot, which slows you down if you're not completing tasks end-to-end.</p><p id="07d5604c-15ef-489c-abda-4c76cd70c7da">As engineers adapt to higher daily output and multi-threaded collaboration with agents, they need to build new mental habits around multitasking and asynchronous review, which is a different cognitive exercise from traditional coding.</p><p id="07d5604c-15ef-489c-abda-4c76cd70c7da">It's a wider scope. At the end of the day, you feel you were more focused, but not in the way when you're coding and have to be in the zone for extended periods.</p><p>Crafting code was a skill that you built, and not many people had it. It kind of felt like a superpower of being able to create something from scratch and code it yourself. If you're really into the code-crafting piece, it's a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/software-engineering-job-technical-interviews-hiring-ai-2026-7">big change that some engineers struggle</a> with.</p><p>At the end of the day, it felt lighter. Now with the management of agents, it's faster-paced.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/cisco-director-engineering-ai-agents-faster-work-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>Micro dramas are weird, cheap, soap operas for your phone. And they're booming.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T09:30:06Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/micro-drama-explained-candyjar-ali-albazaz-interview-peter-kafka-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a91ada179f11f0a89f9223d?format=jpeg" height="1500" width="2000" alt="A photo treatment featuring hands holding a phone displaying a Micro-drama from Candy Jar"><figcaption><p class="copyright">CandyJar; Getty Images; BI</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Micro dramas should be easy to ignore: How big could the market be for low-budget soap operas, designed to be consumed in one-minute chunks?</li><li>Pretty big, it turns out: Possibly $14 billion a year.</li><li>Much of that comes from China, where micro dramas started. But US apps like CandyJar say they're seeing real growth. And TikTok is looming …</li></ul><p>What if you could watch short videos on your phone? What if you could pay people to watch those videos?</p><p>I know, I know: I'm describing <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/inside-quibis-175-billion-rise-and-six-month-fall-2020-10">Quibi</a>, the infamous app that flopped in 2020.</p><p>But: I'm also describing micro dramas — low-budget movies cut into one-minute chunks. And those do seem to be working: Consumers may be spending as much as $14 billion on them this year.</p><p>Most of that spending is happening in China, where the genre took off. But <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/micro-dramas-hollywood-peacock-hbo-streaming-service-challengers-2025-10">micro dramas are breaking through in the US</a>, too: Mainstream video platforms like <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/peacock-reelshort-micro-dramas-bravo-hollywood-short-form-vertical-video-2026-5">Peacock</a> are adding them to the mix, and US-based companies like <a target="_blank" href="https://candyjar.com/">CandyJar</a> say they're seeing very fast growth as well.</p><p>It may be that micro dramas have limited appeal, and won't grow beyond their current audience — primarily women looking for quick diversions, via Harlequin-style romances. But even if micro dramas end there, they would still represent a real change in the way at least some Americans get, and pay for, entertainment.</p><p>Ali Albazaz thinks they will become much bigger: He's the CEO of <a target="_blank" href="https://www.inkitt.com/">Inkitt</a>, a startup that began as a platform for amateur writers, which is now morphing into a micro drama player. It's the company that owns CandyJar, and which has also launched <a target="_blank" href="https://ironblood.com/">Ironblood</a>, a micro drama vendor aimed at dudes who are happy to watch AI-generated action/adventure tales.</p><p>I think also think it's possible that micro dramas get truly big in the US. But it's also possible to imagine that when that happens, the industry will be dominated by TikTok and Meta's Reels.</p><p>Those platforms are already the main way apps like CandyJar find their customers. So why not just keep the whole thing for themselves?</p><p>And indeed, <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/tiktok-jumps-into-micro-dramas-buzzy-bite-sized-soaps-2025-12">TikTok</a> is trying out multiple ways to tackle micro dramas, including a <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/tiktok-launches-a-new-micro-drama-app-called-pinedrama-2026-1">free, ad-supported app</a>, as well as a <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/tiktok-testing-paid-micro-drama-app-costs-20-a-month-2026-7">paid version</a>.</p><p>"The competition is ruthless," Albazaz acknowledges. "There is risk and threat from every side."</p><p>Albazaz walked me through micro drama economics and audience in the most recent episode of my <a target="_blank" href="https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/channels-with-peter-kafka/id1080467174">Channels</a> podcast, which also included an industry overview from Hernan Lopez, who runs the <a target="_blank" href="https://www.owlandco.com/">Owl &amp; Co</a>. entertainment consultancy. You can hear both conversations in their entirety <a target="_blank" href="https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-weird-big-business-of-microdramas/id1080467174?i=1000786031911">here</a>. The following is an edited excerpt of my talk with Albazaz.</p><p><strong>Peter Kafka: There's no shortage of short-form entertainment out there. Reels and TikTok give it to me for free, and they tune it to what I want.</strong></p><p><strong>What are micro dramas providing that isn't already there, and why do people pay to watch them?</strong></p><p><strong>Ali Albazaz:</strong> The user-generated content that you get on TikTok and so on don't do serialized content. So you don't have full dramas being told.</p><p>Micro dramas really taught us that you can chop the movie into 90-second-long episodes and then sell individual episodes or a subscription.</p><p><strong>What's your budget for these shows?</strong></p><p>It costs about $200,000 to do a physical production in Los Angeles at this point. You can go from $150,000 to $300,000. We tend to be at the higher end.</p><p><strong>Does the production value matter to consumers? A lot of the stuff I see seems to be … the polite word, I guess, is "inexpensive." It seems like people are quite comfortable with that. What is the urge to up the ante on your end?</strong></p><p>You're correct to say that the majority of micro dramas look [like] very low-quality. But we really have very high expectations from our team, and we really want to stand out that way.</p><p><strong>CandyJar, and most micro dramas, are aimed towards women. You also recently launched </strong><a target="_blank" href="https://ironblood.com/"><strong>Ironblood</strong></a><strong> — action/adventure aimed at men. With those shows, you really lean into the idea that you're making them with AI. Why is that important to disclose, and are you worried about AI pushback?</strong></p><p>AI is allowing us to create movies that would normally be predominantly-CGI based, very, very cheaply.</p><p><strong>You can't afford Marvel-level CGI, but you can do an AI version of it.</strong></p><p>That's right. We had so many great stories that are superhero and action-based, and previously it would cost us $200 million to go out and produce them.</p><p><strong>But some people who are using AI try to hide it, and if it comes out that they're using it, it's a scandal. You guys clearly don't think that's a problem.</strong></p><p>We don't want to lie, right? We want to be open and honest with our users.</p><p><strong>Do these adventure stories that you're telling on Ironblood have the same budget as the romances you're showing on CandyJar?</strong></p><p>No. They end up being significantly cheaper. We're talking $10,000 to $50,000.</p><p><strong>What's the future of your business? Figuring out other micro drama formats? Or trying to branch out into things like traditional TV shows and movies?</strong></p><p>We're building the operating system for storytellers, whether they want to create a bestselling book, audiobook, or movie.</p><p>We want to have movies that you can watch in the cinema. We want to create theme parks at some point. The idea is to really help storytellers tell their stories in all possible formats.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/micro-drama-explained-candyjar-ali-albazaz-interview-peter-kafka-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>I spoke to 6 people who bounced back from a career break. These 3 lessons stuck with me.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T11:03:19Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/3-lessons-career-breaks-bounced-back-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a940d7779f11f0a89f92861?format=jpeg" height="4000" width="6000" alt="Natasya Pawanteh in. red shirt sitting on a table with food"><figcaption>Natasya Pawanteh pivoted careers after caring for her parents.<p class="copyright">Joshua Paul for BI</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Business Insider's reporter Charissa Cheong spent hours interview people who took career breaks.</li><li>She turned the interviews into her series My Big Break, which explores how the people bounced back.</li><li>She learned a lot from the interviewees, including how sacrifice can be character-building.</li></ul><p>Over the past four months, I've spent hours interviewing people who were brave enough to take a career break.</p><p>I wanted to know if and how they overcame the many obstacles <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/internship-career-break-returner-tech-raise-son-2025-9">career returners</a> face when trying to crack the job market. It all built up to the series <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/career-break-success-stories-2026-8">My Big Break</a>, which told a diverse range of stories, from stepping away to care for a child with autism, caring for parents until their final breaths, and moving to another country with family and leaving a job behind.</p><p>As someone who isn't planning a career break any time soon,<strong> </strong>one thing I didn't expect was to learn so much from the people who shared their stories with me. Although their journeys weren't always smooth, I took comfort in seeing how they adapted, found ways to move forward in their careers, and learned lessons that shaped their character.</p><p>Here are three lessons I learned.</p><h2 id="12b3e6cb-cb06-423c-acde-8f1200d31d53" data-toc-id="12b3e6cb-cb06-423c-acde-8f1200d31d53">1. Your network can help your career comeback</h2><p>In my fantasy career break, I'd be offline and unplugged as much as possible. But the more interviews I did, the more I noticed how big a difference staying in touch with one's network can make in a comeback.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a908ea345e6f385a5169ed0?format=jpeg" height="1024" width="1366" alt="Nicki Schroeder"><figcaption>Nicki Schroeder took a career break to care for her daughter.<p class="copyright">Hanna-Katrina Jedrosz for BI</p></figcaption></figure><p>When Nicki Schroeder, a UK-based media lawyer, tried to re-enter her industry after 10 years, her contacts helped her get back up to speed, meaning she was prepared for her <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/10-year-career-break-care-for-daughter-back-work-2026-6">successful job interview</a>. The same contacts then equipped her with a list of key precedents decided while she was out of the workforce.</p><p>Talking to Schroeder made me reflect on how significant help from people you know and trust can be, especially when you feel a bit rusty after taking time off.</p><p>In the case of Ramya Ramesh, a semiconductor professional who worried she'd never get another job after a six-year career break, her former colleagues encouraged her to <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/returner-program-career-break-tech-industry-2026-7">apply for an opportunity</a> in her old department. Meanwhile, Adam Stewart, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/google-career-break-reset-2026-7">an ex-Googler</a> who took an eight-month break, said that he turned to former colleagues for advice about his next steps, while also making new connections.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a60e2aa548c9c486b30f0e3?format=jpeg" height="2667" width="4000" alt="Ramya Ramesh"><figcaption>Ramya Ramesh took advantage of her previous employer&#39;s returner program.<p class="copyright">Brian W. Fraser for BI</p></figcaption></figure><h2 id="46f3cc12-84e1-4044-9bb5-8453d8189b46" data-toc-id="46f3cc12-84e1-4044-9bb5-8453d8189b46">2. A career break is an opportunity to open yourself up to new things</h2><p>Not all of the people I spoke to returned to their original industry.<strong> </strong>Mounika Chinnam and Natasya Pawanteh both felt reentering their industries would be challenging after long absences.</p><p>The tech industry had transformed significantly during Chinnam's seven-year break, so she was open to non-technical jobs. Becoming <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/stay-at-home-mom-career-break-internship-2026-8">an intern</a> for a digital marketing company at 31 with colleagues who were younger than her felt a little strange, but it enabled her to land a full-time role in a new industry.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a940ded79f11f0a89f92864?format=jpeg" height="4000" width="6000" alt="Office worker at a desk uses multiple screens in front of a whiteboard and office supplies."><figcaption>Natasya Pawanteh changes careers.<p class="copyright">Joshua Paul for BI</p></figcaption></figure><p>Pawanteh thought it would be an uphill battle getting anyone in geology to give her a chance after a seven-year break. She tried volunteering, leading to her transition into nonprofit work.</p><p>Seeing how happy Pawanteh and Chinnam seemed in their new industries, which they may not have landed in had they not taken a career break, made me consider the value of trying new things and keeping an open mind.</p><p>I felt similarly inspired when I met Glenn Stephenson, who took a break from his "safe" <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/took-sabbatical-pwc-co-found-business-2026-6">career at PwC</a> to experiment with his own business. I like to think of myself as open to new things, but seeing someone take such a big leap made me question how far I'd go to explore an idea or passion.</p><h2 id="f8683eb7-e02f-450d-bfb6-131e6fcc95f0" data-toc-id="f8683eb7-e02f-450d-bfb6-131e6fcc95f0">3. Sacrifice can be character-building</h2><p>I'm still at a relatively early stage in my career, and my friends and I often discuss whether we'd want to pause work when we have kids. I've never been sure how to answer, partly because my parents worked while I was growing up.</p><p>Meeting people like Schroeder and Pawanteh, who stepped back to <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/career-break-care-for-parents-new-job-2026-8">become carers</a>, gave me an insight into the costs and sacrifices that come with pausing a fruitful career to invest in someone else.</p><p>Hearing about the energy and effort they expended, I felt challenged by how, as good as having a fulfilling job is, our collective focus on climbing corporate ladders, getting promoted, and garnering likes on LinkedIn can make us quite self-centered. It's something Pawanteh captured well when she talked about why she decided not to return to her geology career.</p><p>To quote from her as-told-to essay: "I'd loved geology since I was 16, but I realized I had a selfish outlook on life, all about me, me, me. Caring for my parents made me realize what it's like to be present for another human being."</p><p>Her story in particular made me hope that, if there came a time when a loved one needed me, I'd have the love and selflessness required to put my career aside for them.</p><p>As Pawanteh said of her parents in her as-told-to essay: "It was a privilege to look after them until the end of their days, and I think that will be the greatest achievement of my life."</p><p><strong>You can read all the stories mentioned here in Business Insider's series, </strong><a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/career-break-success-stories-2026-8"><strong>My Big Break</strong></a><strong>.</strong></p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/3-lessons-career-breaks-bounced-back-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>It's Warren Buffett's 96th birthday. His last year was one of the most transformational yet.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T09:30:03Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-birthday-96-alphabet-stocks-investing-philanthropy-berkshire-retirement-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a90561379f11f0a89f9194a?format=jpeg" height="2055" width="3000" alt="Warren Buffett"><figcaption>Warren Buffett is Berkshire Hathaway&#39;s chairman and former CEO.<p class="copyright">Daniel Zuchnik/WireImage</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Warren Buffett celebrates his 96th birthday on Sunday.</li><li>He's retired as CEO, bet big on Alphabet, and ramped up his giving over the past 12 months.</li><li>Here are the highlights from the legendary investor's landmark year.</li></ul><p>Happy birthday, Mr. Buffett.</p><p><a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-95-birthday-berkshire-hathaway-stock-investing-025-8">Investing legend Warren Buffett</a> turns 96 on Sunday, and the 12 months since his 95th birthday have been truly transformational, featuring a huge career move and a major new investment. He's also accelerated his charitable giving and dispensed plenty of his trademark wit and wisdom.</p><h2 id="26b6c3e2-b797-4841-b9f2-a24fdc38cd94" data-toc-id="26b6c3e2-b797-4841-b9f2-a24fdc38cd94">Into the next chapter</h2><p>For his <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-letter-ceo-retirement-berkshire-stock-abel-thanksgiving-philanthropy-2025-11">Thanksgiving message</a>, Buffett penned a love letter to his hometown of Omaha, reflected on his good fortune, and thanked the many people who helped him throughout his life.</p><p>Buffett, who has pledged to donate virtually all of his wealth to good causes, said he would <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-thanksgiving-letter-berkshire-stock-abel-succession-retirement-2025-11">speed up his giving</a> as he wanted his children to be the ones who distribute his fortune.</p><p>He also encouraged his followers to learn from their mistakes, choose good role models, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-life-advice-decide-your-obituary-thanksgiving-letter-2025-11">live up to the obituaries</a> they want for themselves, and care for others.</p><p>"When you help someone in any of thousands of ways, you help the world," he wrote. "Kindness is costless but also priceless."</p><p>Buffett <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-berkshire-ceo-retirement-greg-abel-challenges-cash-dividend-2026-1">retired</a> as Berkshire Hathaway CEO at the end of December after six decades in charge. He remains chairman of the company, which he transformed from a failing textile mill into a $1 trillion juggernaut.</p><h2 id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e" data-toc-id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">Sharing life lessons</h2><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">Buffett <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-life-advice-debt-mistakes-parenting-jobs-interview-berkshire-2026-1 ">shared</a> several pieces of life advice during a CNBC interview aired in January but filmed in May 2025.</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">The billionaire warned against <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-on-margin-debt-for-stocks-investing-2018-2">getting into debt</a> as it leaves people "underwater" and unable to escape.</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">He urged parents to practice what they preach and <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/leon-cooperman-stocks-economy-outlook-warren-buffett-life-advice-billionaire-2025-6">set good examples</a> for their kids: "If you want to have good children, be a good parent."</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">Buffett also recommended people <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-95-birthday-berkshire-hathaway-retirement-work-careers-philanthropy-2025-8">find jobs they love</a> so much that the "paycheck is incidental to what you're doing."</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">The bargain hunter also <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-cnbc-interview-berkshire-hathaway-deals-acquisitions-cash-investing-2026-1 ">vented</a> about high asset prices constraining him from deploying Berkshire's capital, which has caused its cash pile to balloon.</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">He said he'd be "willing to spend $100 billion this afternoon," as he'd much rather have that money in a&nbsp;<a target="_blank" href="https://markets.businessinsider.com/news/stocks/warren-buffett-berkshire-hathaway-russia-ukraine-stocks-gold-bitcoin-dollars-2022-2">quality business</a>&nbsp;than in cash.</p><h2 id="1aeac0e4-0703-41c9-b145-e133a64f9fbf" data-toc-id="1aeac0e4-0703-41c9-b145-e133a64f9fbf">The past and the present</h2><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">Berkshire's&nbsp;<a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/greg-abel-shareholder-letter-warren-buffett-berkshire-ceo-succession-tribute-2026-2">annual report</a>&nbsp;highlighted Buffett's remarkable track record: Berkshire stock rose by about 6,100,000% between 1965 and 2025, trouncing the S&amp;P 500's roughly 46,100% return, including dividends, over the same period.</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">It also showed the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-greg-abel-stock-picks-investing-apple-coke-amex-2026-3 ">power of Buffett's stock picks</a>. Berkshire's Apple stake was worth 10 times its cost base at the end of December. Coca-Cola was up 21-fold, American Express was up 45-fold, and Moody's was up 51-fold.</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">In a March interview with CNBC, Buffett said his <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-greg-abel-stocks-berkshire-philanthropy-interview-billionaire-2026-3 ">life hadn't changed</a> much since retiring as CEO. He's still commuting to Berkshire's headquarters in downtown Omaha five days a week, and continuing to pick stocks and field calls about potential acquisitions, albeit with his successor Greg Abel having the final say.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/68e3bfb35dbc4fd10daa3bb2?format=jpeg" height="3815" width="5723" alt="Warren Buffett"><figcaption>Warren Buffett is still picking stocks and going to the office.<p class="copyright">Nati Harnik/AP</p></figcaption></figure><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">Buffett also sat for a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-surprise-interview-berkshire-hathaway-meeting-gambling-nuclear-deepfakes-2026-5 ">surprise interview</a> during Berkshire's annual shareholder meeting in May. He warned of a "gambling mood" in markets, describing it as a "church with a casino attached."</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">He said it was "not an ideal environment" for deploying cash, so he and his team were having to "pick our spots."</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">Buffett also cracked a few jokes, replying when asked whether he'd met the new managers of some of Berkshire's key holdings: "I haven't met the old managers."</p><h2 id="b9569e29-b2ad-4345-9e22-da02b009f0a3" data-toc-id="b9569e29-b2ad-4345-9e22-da02b009f0a3">Still in the mix</h2><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">In his July letter about his philanthropy, Buffett said he <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-berkshire-hathaway-stock-philanthropy-foundations-death-gates-foundation-2026-7 ">hoped</a> to distribute his entire Berkshire fortune, over $140 billion, to good causes by the end of 2034.</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">Buffett also <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-berkshire-hathaway-stock-philanthropy-foundations-death-gates-foundation-2026-7 ">told</a> CNBC at the time that he'd "read a great deal" about his friend Bill Gates' ties to Jeffrey Epstein, and that while it was a "distasteful" situation, everyone makes mistakes when judging people.</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">In the same interview, Buffett said he <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-berkshire-alphabet-investment-goog-ai-tech-stocks-2026-7">made the surprising call</a> to invest in Alphabet last summer. Berkshire built that stake from scratch to nearly $38 billion by the end of June, making Google's parent company the third-biggest position in its stock portfolio after Apple and American Express.</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">If Buffett is still behind that bet — likely given his early involvement, the size of the wager, and his confirmation that he's still picking stocks as chairman — it could be his <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-berkshire-ai-alphabet-tech-stock-portfolio-google-cash-2026-8">last big play</a>.</p><p id="447589d0-3ba4-42a2-aae2-19f24d5c780e">Weeks away from his 96th birthday, Buffett <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-luck-age-wealth-investing-stock-market-berkshire-hathaway-2026-7 ">said</a> he felt fortunate to be alive and healthy, and while he was "losing marbles," he'd "accumulated marbles for a longer time than I deserved, and that's just a matter of luck."</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/warren-buffett-birthday-96-alphabet-stocks-investing-philanthropy-berkshire-retirement-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>OpenAI and Anthropic are battling Big Tech for talent. We asked workers who's winning them over — and who's not.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T09:30:02Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/tech-workers-dream-employers-openai-anthropic-apple-google-amazon-jobs-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a887a998a99fa493d60edec?format=jpeg" height="1500" width="2000" alt="Mike Kostersitz (left), Abhinav Bohra (center), and Sneja Shah (right)"><figcaption>Mike Kostersitz (left), Abhinav Bohra (center), and Sneja Shah (right) shared their dream employers and the companies they might pass on.<p class="copyright">Mike Kostersitz (left), Abhinav Bohra (center), and Sneja Shah (right)</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Tech companies are competing fiercely for workers who can help them win the AI race.</li><li>We asked eight tech workers for their dream employers — and the companies they'd pass on.</li><li>Some favored OpenAI or Anthropic, while others preferred Big Tech.</li></ul><p>While tech companies are pouring <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/big-tech-earnings-microsoft-ai-investment-capex-plan-2026-4">billions into AI infrastructure</a>, they are also competing <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/apple-lawsuit-openai-trade-secrets-what-smart-people-are-saying-2026-7">fiercely for AI talent</a> — and the AI boom is reshaping the choices available to workers.</p><p>Alongside established giants like Apple, Google, and Amazon, frontier AI labs like <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/openai-anthropic-warning-about-future-they-are-building-2026-6">OpenAI and Anthropic</a> now offer the chance to work at the edge of a technological shift, with potentially significant financial upside. Meanwhile, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/visa-holders-immigrants-big-tech-layoffs-job-security-work-careers-2026-8">years of tech layoffs</a> have made job security a bigger consideration for many workers.</p><p>We asked eight tech workers about their dream employer, the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/charts-show-employee-count-changing-big-tech-companies-2026-7">Big Tech companies</a> they're most and least interested in, and whether they've <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/best-worst-places-to-build-tech-career-2026-8">pursued jobs</a> at OpenAI or Anthropic. (Their responses have been edited for length and clarity.)</p><h2 id="d6bb6c53-a45e-4947-ac5d-fb3e4ad57751" data-toc-id="d6bb6c53-a45e-4947-ac5d-fb3e4ad57751">AI labs have come calling. I haven't pursued them.</h2><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8c7f6c8a99fa493d60f80b?format=jpeg" height="720" width="960" alt="Abhinav Bohra"><figcaption>Abhinav Bohra says he&#39;d choose Amazon, with NVIDIA as his runner-up.<p class="copyright">Abhinav Bohra</p></figcaption></figure><p><em>Abhinav Bohra is a senior applied scientist at Amazon. He's in his 30s and lives in Seattle.</em></p><p><strong>Have you tried to land a job at an AI lab like OpenAI or Anthropic?</strong></p><p>A couple of recruiters for <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/openai-meta-superintelligence-lab-work-culture-lessons-applied-researcher-prakhar-2026-3">AI labs</a> have reached out to me, including one at another Big Tech company. I took the calls but never pursued them.</p><p>Labs hire people to make models smarter. I build recommendation engines, and a frontier lab has no real use for one yet: no catalog, no sellers, no shoppers to rank for. The day one of them runs an actual marketplace, people like me get very interested in them. We're not there yet.</p><p><strong>Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?</strong></p><p>Amazon, which is boring, so here's the runner-up: NVIDIA. Recommendation at scale has become an inference cost problem. Running a big model once is cheap. Running it for every search and every shopper in real time is where the money goes. When your unit of progress is the millisecond, NVIDIA sits upstream of everything.</p><p>Each company could be a good fit for someone in my field, but I also imagine they all have teams I'd love and teams I'd dread.</p><h2 id="ffd68ec8-6713-45b0-a641-469d74a0aaa8" data-toc-id="ffd68ec8-6713-45b0-a641-469d74a0aaa8"><strong>I'd choose Anthropic for its values</strong></h2><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a886d7e8a99fa493d60ed04?format=jpeg" height="720" width="960" alt="Mike Kostersitz"><figcaption>Mike Kostersitz says Anthropic would be his dream employer outside Nike.<p class="copyright">Mike Kostersitz</p></figcaption></figure><p><em>Mike Kostersitz is a senior director, product management at Nike. He's in his early 60s and lives in Oregon.</em></p><p><strong>If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?</strong></p><p>If I had to look outside Nike, Anthropic would be my dream employer. The pull is real, and the company's stated values align more closely with my own than some other companies.</p><p>I took note when earlier this year, Anthropic refused a Pentagon push to <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-claude-ai-military-use-dario-amodei-2026-2">strip out restrictions</a> on mass surveillance and autonomous weapons use, a stand their own CFO said could cost the company <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-face-loss-in-dispute-with-pentagon-openai-2026-3">billions in revenue</a>. That's the kind of "values over dollars" moment most companies only talk about.</p><p>I don't expect that to hold forever. <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/openai-anthropic-ai-ipo-spacex-stocks-stock-market-investing-trade-2026-6">Once they IPO</a>, the pull toward shareholder value will grow, and I'd expect other priorities to erode over time as a result. But I'd still pick Anthropic as my top choice.</p><p><strong>Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?</strong></p><p>Apple, hands down, I love the products and what the culture represents. Least would be Amazon. I have a number of friends who are current or former <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/amazon-employees-layoffs-ai-return-to-office-rto-tracking-2026-5">Amazon employees</a> on the tech side, and not one of them has ever seemed excited to go to work there or felt like they were making a difference, beyond the paycheck being strong.</p>
      
      <aside class="callout-box headline-regular ignore-typography">
        
        <p>Business Insider is speaking with tech workers who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads — whether due to a layoff, resignation, job search, or shifting workplace expectations.</p><p><strong>Share your story</strong> by <a target="_blank" rel=" nofollow" class="" href="https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSechTVqVWQve8iqYssNriCXdtwwdgGRixNNZpmslSKBQqIJ8g/viewform?usp=header">filling out this form</a>.</p>
      
      </aside>
    
    <h2 id="ba9693e7-3ff6-44a2-b797-bb9569db8bb5" data-toc-id="ba9693e7-3ff6-44a2-b797-bb9569db8bb5"><strong>I haven't applied to OpenAI or Anthropic</strong></h2><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8c82ed1d1a1d028ba125da?format=jpeg" height="3264" width="4352" alt="Meta"><figcaption>Meta&#39;s scale is part of its appeal in the competition for AI talent.<p class="copyright">Imen Ben Youssef / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><p><em>This tech worker is a software engineer at Meta.</em></p><p><strong>If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?</strong></p><p>Honestly, the answer might be where I already am: Meta. The frontier labs get the headlines, but hyperscalers like Meta and Google are doing the same caliber of work: not just core model training and fine-tuning but building the insane infrastructure needed to serve this to billions of users.</p><p>One reason I haven't tried to land a job at an AI lab like OpenAI or Anthropic is that the labs are <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-1-5-trillion-valuation-on-secondary-markets-2026-8">running on investor capital</a>, while the hyperscalers fund their AI push from core businesses that already make enormous money. They have different risk profiles, and I've been happy with mine.</p><p><strong>Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?</strong></p><p>Most: Setting Meta aside, Google is the obvious choice for me. It's one of the few companies doing everything in-house, from TPUs to <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/google-ai-agent-openclaw-remy-gemini-assistant-2026-5">frontier models</a> to products. That full stack under one roof is appealing.</p><p>Least: Probably Apple, and honestly that's about fit, not the company. They <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/apple-products-that-define-ceo-tim-cook-era-2026-4">build incredible products</a> and their engineering is world class, but their working model is very different from what I'm used to. Teams there tend to work on a focused slice under a lot of confidentiality, while my career so far has been end-to-end ownership, seeing a system from design through production and operations.</p><h2 id="db36bbe5-6500-4aea-8ab5-9bc1ce2197c4" data-toc-id="db36bbe5-6500-4aea-8ab5-9bc1ce2197c4"><strong>I'd choose SpaceX over any Big Tech company or AI lab</strong></h2><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a74708d0c6c5a263f3a6eb0?format=jpeg" height="4000" width="5878" alt="SpaceX rocket"><figcaption>A tech lead (not pictured) in the insurance industry says SpaceX is his dream employer,<p class="copyright">Justin Sullivan/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><p><em>This tech worker is a tech lead at a company in the insurance industry. He's in his early 40s and lives in Atlanta.</em></p><p><strong>If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?</strong></p><p>If I could work for any tech company tomorrow, I'd choose SpaceX. Few organizations on the planet operate with that level of ambition, engineering rigor, and mission clarity. Being part of a team pushing toward <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/spacex-big-falcon-spaceship-construction-musk-mars-missions-2018-9">interplanetary travel</a> would be an opportunity to contribute to something far bigger than any one company.</p><p><strong>Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?</strong></p><p>NVIDIA is the company I would choose. It is defining the future of accelerated computing and AI rather than reacting to it.</p><h2 id="1ffb0845-86ed-48f8-b88c-df079bafa01f" data-toc-id="1ffb0845-86ed-48f8-b88c-df079bafa01f"><strong>NVIDIA and the AI labs are compelling, but I'd still choose Google</strong></h2><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8875d71d1a1d028ba11ba3?format=jpeg" height="540" width="720" alt="Sachin Jain"><figcaption>Sachin Jain says he&#39;d still choose Google, despite the appeal of NVIDIA and leading AI labs.<p class="copyright">Sachin Jain</p></figcaption></figure><p><em>Sachin Jain is a data analyst at Google.</em></p><p><strong>If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?</strong></p><p>It would still be Google, and I'm genuinely grateful that I get to work there. That said, OpenAI and Anthropic would be incredibly compelling as well. They're at the forefront of one of the biggest technological shifts of our generation, and I think any engineer or data professional would find that exciting.</p><p><strong>Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?</strong></p><p>Aside from Google, I'd probably say NVIDIA. They've built an incredible competitive moat by creating a level of dependency across the AI ecosystem that's hard to match.</p><p>Beyond the business itself, I've always admired the culture they've cultivated. Employees don't seem to be constantly looking over their shoulders, worried about the next round of layoffs, which is becoming increasingly rare in tech. And of course, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-social-media-era-2026-8">Jensen Huang</a> is someone I really respect.</p><h2 id="235953fc-019d-4615-8169-6738fda6d5a2" data-toc-id="235953fc-019d-4615-8169-6738fda6d5a2"><strong>I'd rather work at a smaller employer than the hottest tech company</strong></h2><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8c841c8a99fa493d60f846?format=jpeg" height="4972" width="6629" alt="remote worker"><figcaption>A software engineer (not pictured) says she&#39;d rather have meaningful ownership at a smaller company than work for a prestigious tech giant.<p class="copyright">aire images/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><p><em>This tech worker is a software engineer at a startup. She's in her 20s and lives in the Northeast.</em></p><p><strong>If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?</strong></p><p>What I value most today is a remote-first environment, the ability to influence what gets built, and a culture where I can spend my time solving interesting technical problems instead of navigating constant internal politics. At this stage of my career, I'd rather work at a smaller company where I have meaningful ownership than be one person in a very large organization.</p><p>Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic are particularly high on my list. I'm not especially motivated by working at whichever company is getting the most attention at the moment. Prestige and compensation alone aren't what motivate my career decisions anymore.</p><p><strong>Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?</strong></p><p>I'd probably lean toward Alphabet, Microsoft, or Apple, but the specific role would matter much more than the company name. I'm less drawn to Meta than some of the others because it has gone through significant organizational changes and layoffs in recent years.</p><h2 id="c374c770-d05e-4863-b565-e45af7ad89e8" data-toc-id="c374c770-d05e-4863-b565-e45af7ad89e8"><strong>Anthropic is my dream employer — I'd maybe pass on Microsoft</strong></h2><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8c84768a99fa493d60f852?format=jpeg" height="3000" width="4000" alt="Anthropic"><figcaption>Anthropic&#39;s focus on enterprise AI is part of its appeal to some tech workers.<p class="copyright">Illustration by Sheldon Cooper/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><p><em>This tech worker works for a large tech company.</em></p><p><strong>If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?</strong></p><p>If I could walk into any company tomorrow, it would be Anthropic. I like that they are going after the enterprise side and actually improving specific lines of business, not just shipping a chatbot. And with the talk of them heading toward public markets, the upside is hard to ignore.</p><p><strong>Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?</strong></p><p>Most to least: Amazon, Alphabet, NVIDIA, Apple, Meta, and Microsoft last.</p><p>Microsoft is last for me because I think they are behind on AI, and it shows on the consumer product side. Copilot, from my own use and from what I hear in the market, has not landed the way it should and people are underwhelmed.</p><h2 id="cfcece07-e1e9-4b66-ae30-63cf0d997bef" data-toc-id="cfcece07-e1e9-4b66-ae30-63cf0d997bef"><strong>OpenAI tops my list</strong></h2><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a886df68a99fa493d60ed15?format=jpeg" height="768" width="1024" alt="Sneja Shah"><figcaption>Sneja Shah says OpenAI would be her top choice outside her current employer.<p class="copyright">Sneja Shah</p></figcaption></figure><p><em>Sneja Shah is a senior technical program manager at the software company Red Hat. She's in her 30s and lives in California.</em></p><p><strong>If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?</strong></p><p>If I had to look outside my current employer, OpenAI would be my top choice. The opportunity to work on products that are fundamentally changing how people work, learn, and create is incredibly exciting.</p><p>Anthropic would also be high on my list because of its emphasis on responsible AI development and long-term safety.</p><p><strong>Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?</strong></p><p>Among those companies, I'd choose NVIDIA because it's enabling nearly every major <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/quantum-computing-stocks-nvidia-ising-ai-xndu-inoq-rgti-qbts-2026-4">advancement in AI</a>. Microsoft would be a close second because of how rapidly it's integrating AI across enterprise products and productivity tools.</p><p><em>Do you have a story to share? Reach out to the reporter via email at </em><a target="_blank" href="mailto:jzinkula@businessinsider.com"><em><u>jzinkula@businessinsider.com</u></em></a><em>, or via Signal at jzinkula.29.</em></p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/tech-workers-dream-employers-openai-anthropic-apple-google-amazon-jobs-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>I help people retire abroad. How to decide if it's the right move, and how to prepare.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T09:30:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/want-to-retire-abroad-how-to-decide-prepare-relocation-expert-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a881faa8a99fa493d60eae7?format=jpeg" height="950" width="1266" alt="Federica Grazi headshot"><figcaption>Federica Grazi said people are often attracted by lifestyles abroad, but don&#39;t always consider the finer details.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Federica Grazi</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Retiring abroad requires more than choosing where to live.</li><li>Federica Grazi, who helps retirees relocate, shared her advice for deciding whether to move and how to plan.</li><li>She says trial stays and healthcare planning are vital before relocating.</li></ul><p><em>This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Federica Grazi, 34, who is based in London. She is the founder of Mitos Relocation Solutions, an advisory firm that helps retirees move abroad. It has been edited for length and clarity.</em></p><p>There's often a big gap between people who <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/americans-spending-retirement-living-in-different-countries-things-to-know-2025-1">dream of retiring abroad</a> and those who actually take the first step toward it. For many, hesitation gets in the way, and the idea of moving remains a dream.</p><p>People are often drawn abroad by the lifestyle, but <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/couple-left-america-moved-abroad-retired-in-huahin-thailand-affordable-2026-5">making a successful move</a> means considering the full picture, like healthcare, aging, and the tax implications of residing in a new location.</p><p>Here are the five things I recommend everyone do before they retire abroad.</p><h2 id="0744fa4c-0804-4595-9411-bcc1988d223e" data-toc-id="0744fa4c-0804-4595-9411-bcc1988d223e"><strong>1. Test-drive your potential new home</strong></h2><p id="0744fa4c-0804-4595-9411-bcc1988d223e">Spend an <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/americans-tried-living-abroad-mexico-lessons-proved-we-could-2025-9">extended trial period</a>, say three months, in the place you're thinking of moving to. It's not about visiting for a week in July or August. Go in the offseason and try living like a local, thinking about what your everyday life would look like.</p><p>Rent an apartment, speak with locals and expats, and join community Facebook groups.</p><p>I've had clients for whom something as simple as getting medication from a pharmacy became an important test of whether they could see themselves living somewhere.</p><h2 id="4e64092b-7751-4d42-9d6e-95ceeb34a5cd" data-toc-id="4e64092b-7751-4d42-9d6e-95ceeb34a5cd"><strong>2. Turn the dream into a decision</strong></h2><p>If you're unsure about retiring abroad, it doesn't have to be all or nothing. The key is not to let inertia take over and leave it as a dream, but to move from a question mark to a clear yes or no.</p><p>In addition to spending a trial period in the country, you can do smaller things like speaking to others who have already moved to the destination to understand how it works in practice, or get advice from an expert who can give you a full rundown. They could even go on a scouting trip for you.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a881fde8a99fa493d60eaec?format=jpeg" height="2500" width="3750" alt="Federica Grazi speaks at Silver Marketing Association conference"><figcaption>Grazi said people should try to live like a local before moving to a new location.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Federica Grazi</p></figcaption></figure><h2 id="76275abc-1532-4606-91da-6d3be783453c" data-toc-id="76275abc-1532-4606-91da-6d3be783453c"><strong>3. Don't rush</strong></h2><p>If you decide to retire abroad and you're excited about it, don't rush the move. <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/golden-visa-firm-plan-b-passports-middle-class-professional-retiree-2026-8">Changing residency</a> is an important moment, so make a clear plan for what needs to happen before you leave.</p><p>Think about whether you need a visa, housing, and even how you'll move your pet. You should also deal with things that aren't necessarily pleasant, like your will.</p><h2 id="9d0b5f03-81fc-45d4-9ff6-53ba670a5055" data-toc-id="9d0b5f03-81fc-45d4-9ff6-53ba670a5055"><strong>4. Think about taxes</strong></h2><p>People often focus on the lifestyle abroad and think, "I love it here. I'll figure everything else out later." But that can lead to big tax mistakes, which need to be addressed before you move.</p><p>If you only discover a problem after the tax year has ended, there might not be much you can do about it.</p><h2 id="2d03c028-81d2-4777-816e-dc57f56eaea6" data-toc-id="2d03c028-81d2-4777-816e-dc57f56eaea6"><strong>5. Take healthcare seriously</strong></h2><p>Healthcare is something you want to be thinking about before you need it. How do you access it? How much will it cost? What might happen if you end up in the hospital?</p><p>If you wait until something goes wrong, you could find yourself having to react and needing to navigate an unfamiliar <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-from-texas-to-italy-retire-saving-healthcare-costs-2026-3">healthcare system</a> before you're fully integrated.</p><p>Often, when people say they hated living abroad and moved back, it's because they didn't do enough research or preparation beforehand.</p><p>Retirement abroad should be a period of joy and expansion. Doing the planning beforehand means that once you arrive, you can actually enjoy it.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/want-to-retire-abroad-how-to-decide-prepare-relocation-expert-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>A financially independent couple shares 3 money rules that helped them pay off debt and build wealth</title>
    <updated>2026-08-30T09:15:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/3-money-rules-that-helped-one-couple-hit-financial-independence-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a91e0b43f7df8787cff4f22?format=jpeg" height="1352" width="1802" alt="klines"><figcaption>Brittany and Kelan Kline are the cofounders of The Savvy Couple.<p class="copyright">Kelan Kline</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Kelan and Brittany Kline built The Savvy Couple blog into a seven-figure online business success.</li><li>They achieved a $1 million net worth by balancing income growth with controlled lifestyle spending.</li><li>"We make a plan for our money every month," Kelan said.</li></ul><p>For Kelan and Brittany Kline, improving their finances came down to a simple idea: widen the gap between what they earned and what they spent.</p><p>The couple, who once worked traditional jobs as a jail deputy and elementary school teacher, were newly married and carrying roughly $40,000 in student-loan debt when they began <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/savvy-couple-first-steps-to-financial-independence-net-worth-2026-8">rethinking their finances</a>.</p><p>They attacked both sides of the equation. On the income side, they built <a target="_blank" class="" href="https://thesavvycouple.com/">The Savvy Couple</a>, a personal-finance blog that eventually <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/couple-built-seven-figure-business-how-to-make-money-online-2026-8">grew into a seven-figure online business</a>. On the spending side, they focused on keeping their lifestyle relatively stable as their income increased.</p><p>The couple said their household net worth — including the estimated value of their businesses, investments, and primary residence — surpassed $1 million in 2020. Business Insider reviewed a screenshot from their Rocket Money account showing a seven-figure net worth.</p><p>Here are three principles they said helped them spend less without feeling permanently deprived.</p><h3 id="04b448ce-a697-4e26-9ac8-d17b8aff1be7" data-toc-id="04b448ce-a697-4e26-9ac8-d17b8aff1be7">1. Think about what a purchase costs in time</h3><p>One of the biggest shifts for the Klines was mental. They started thinking about purchases not simply in dollars, but in hours of work.</p><p>"We had a realization that, with our 9-to-5s, we were trading our time for money," Kelan told Business Insider. "Every purchase we had, we were not actually paying for it with money. We were actually paying it with our time."</p><p>A $50,000 truck, for example, might represent months of work. A $100 dinner might translate into several hours on the job.</p><p>"It kind of gives you that perspective of, 'Is this worth my time to purchase it?'" he said.</p><h3 id="522984ae-b859-41b1-af27-28b5f47c2c01" data-toc-id="522984ae-b859-41b1-af27-28b5f47c2c01">2. Know the difference between frugal and cheap</h3><p>The Klines don't equate frugality with always buying the least expensive option.</p><p>"There's a very distinct difference between being cheap and frugal," Kelan said.</p><p>A cheap shopper, for example, might buy the least expensive vacuum and have to replace it repeatedly. A frugal shopper, on the other hand, might pay more upfront for something that offers better value and lasts longer.</p><p>The goal, he said, is to ask which option provides the most value without costing unnecessarily more.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a91e0933f7df8787cff4f20?format=jpeg" height="1200" width="1600" alt="klines"><figcaption>The Klines reside in Rochester, New York, where they met in high school.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of The Klines</p></figcaption></figure><p>That mindset also helped them resist lifestyle inflation as their earnings grew. They stayed in their starter home for seven years, drove used cars, rarely ate out, and spent roughly five years as a one-car household.</p><p>"You don't have to increase your lifestyle to be happy," Kelan said. Rather than succumb to lifestyle inflation, they directed more of the growing gap between their income and expenses toward debt repayment and investments.</p><h3 id="c2cf9039-4d9b-45c3-8ba5-fd9d901019e3" data-toc-id="c2cf9039-4d9b-45c3-8ba5-fd9d901019e3">3. Give every dollar a job — including fun money</h3><p>The Klines still track their spending and stick to a monthly budget.</p><p>"We make a plan for our money every month," Kelan said. While some people view budgeting as restrictive, they see it differently: "When you give yourself a budget and make a plan every month, you're actually giving yourself freedom to spend the money where you want it and where you get the most joy and fulfillment from."</p><p>That includes discretionary spending. For example, Brittany enjoys buying coffee, so the couple deliberately builds personal spending money into their budget. Today, they said, each of them gets about $200 a month to spend however they want, up from roughly $100 earlier in their journey.</p><p>The point isn't to eliminate everything enjoyable, but to cut more aggressively in areas that matter less while preserving spending they value.</p><h3 id="b78a1aac-f217-4896-9921-9f69c3fb32d3" data-toc-id="b78a1aac-f217-4896-9921-9f69c3fb32d3">Sometimes the sacrifice is temporary</h3><p>The couple did go through periods of much stricter spending, particularly when they were focused on eliminating their student loans.</p><p>"Sometimes it's temporary pain to get to the end goal that you want," Kelan said. He remembers declining invitations to eat out or meet friends for drinks and cutting restaurant spending to roughly once a month. "We sacrificed a ton when we were paying off debt."</p><p>The key, in his view, was knowing that the restrictions had an endpoint. Rather than thinking they would live that way forever, they treated the cuts as a short-term sprint toward a specific goal.</p><p>Once the debt was gone, money that had previously gone toward loan payments could instead be invested or spent on things they valued more.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/3-money-rules-that-helped-one-couple-hit-financial-independence-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
